September and October bring rtveli, the grape harvest, when every household is pressing. Spring is green and quiet, and winter still works for the churches and towns even though the mountains close. Two days is the honest minimum, three if Tusheti is on the list.
Driving: Two roads lead into Kakheti. The Kakheti Highway through Sagarejo and Badiauri is longer but flat and dependable in any weather. The Gombori Pass road from Tbilisi to Telavi is shorter and much prettier, but it is a genuine mountain crossing with tight bends, and it closes in snow or thick fog — check before choosing it in winter. Inside the valley the asphalt is good and distances between sites are short.

Two sections deserve respect. The final approach to David Gareja is rough, dusty and much easier with ground clearance. The Abano Pass into Tusheti is another matter: an unsurfaced shelf road at 2,850 metres with no barriers, usually open from June to early October, permitted only in a 4x4 and best left to drivers who have done it before.

The other honest warning concerns wine. Tastings are the point of the region and Georgia enforces an effectively zero alcohol limit, so decide who drives before you leave.

### Kvemo Kartli
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/regions/kvemo-kartli/
Kvemo Kartli begins immediately south of Tbilisi and is the region most visitors drive straight through. It repays a day. The landscape shifts quickly, from the industrial plain around Rustavi and the market gardens of Marneuli up onto the Tsalka plateau at around 1,500 metres, where the air is cooler and the villages are built of stone.

Its two headline sites are archaeological rather than scenic. Dmanisi, on a promontory above the meeting of two rivers, produced hominin remains dated to roughly 1.8 million years — the oldest such finds outside Africa — and the ruins of a medieval town stand on the same spur. Bolnisi Sioni, consecrated at the end of the fifth century, is among the oldest surviving churches in the country and carries some of the earliest known inscriptions in the Georgian alphabet.

For a day outdoors there are two good options. Birtvisi is a maze of limestone towers and ravines with a ruined fortress hidden inside it; the walking is genuinely rough and much better with a guide. Dashbashi Canyon above Tsalka is the developed alternative, with a glass viewing bridge over the gorge and a path down towards the waterfalls, and it is the easier choice with children. Algeti National Park, closer to the capital, is quiet spruce forest suited to a short walk rather than a whole day.

This is also the most mixed corner of Georgia: Azerbaijani and Armenian villages sit alongside Georgian ones, and the bread and the cooking change accordingly. Nothing here needs more than a day trip, since everything falls within ninety minutes of Tbilisi.
Driving: The main roads towards Rustavi, Marneuli and Bolnisi are good asphalt and move quickly out of Tbilisi. The difficulty starts on the secondary network. The last few kilometres towards Birtvisi are gravel, and you walk in from there anyway; the climb onto the Tsalka plateau is open and exposed, with snow and ice in winter and frequent low cloud in summer. Ground clearance helps if Birtvisi or village roads are on the plan, while an economy car covers everything else.

Fuel is available in Marneuli, Bolnisi and Tsalka but rarely in the villages between them. Livestock on the road is routine, especially in the evening. One further point: near the Armenian and Azerbaijani frontiers, stay on marked roads — some tracks run straight into the border zone, where driving is not permitted.

### Shida Kartli
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/regions/shida-kartli/
Shida Kartli is the broad middle valley of the Mtkvari, between Tbilisi and the Likhi range. It is one of the most fertile corners of Georgia, with apple and peach orchards running for kilometres, and also the most easily reached: the motorway to Gori is the best road in the country and takes a little over an hour.

The main site is Uplistsikhe, a town carved into soft rock above the left bank of the river. Its history reaches back into the first millennium BC, and what survives today is a stack of halls, wine presses, streets and stairways with a brick basilica of the ninth or tenth century on top. Gori, nine kilometres away, is known for the fortress on its central hill and for the Stalin Museum, which is still arranged largely according to Soviet logic — which is precisely what makes it worth an hour.

Nearby stand two less-visited churches that matter more to art history than to tourist lists. Ateni Sioni, built on the model of Jvari, sits in a narrow vine-growing valley and keeps eleventh-century wall paintings. At Kintsvisi, the frescoes of St Nicholas church — including the celebrated blue angel — count among the peaks of Georgian medieval painting. Samtavisi, right by the highway, is admired for the carved ornament of its eleventh-century facade.

The season is the whole year, since snow does not lie long on the plain. One day covers the three main sites if you leave early, and the region also works as a stop on the way west to Imereti.
Driving: The Tbilisi-Gori section is the best motorway in Georgia: dual carriageway, lit, fast, with a 110 km/h limit and frequent speed cameras. Gori is an hour away, Uplistsikhe another fifteen minutes on good asphalt. An economy car is entirely sufficient for the main circuit.

The branches are harder. The road up the Ateni valley is narrow, in places barely wide enough for one car, and you will be giving way on the bridges. The last kilometres to Kintsvisi are unsurfaced and turn to clay after rain, so ground clearance genuinely helps. On the motorway itself, watch for lorries stopped in the right-hand lane and for tractors joining from village turnings.

One thing matters more than any of that. The administrative boundary line with the occupied Tskhinvali region runs along the north of this region and is not always obviously marked. Do not follow a navigation app blindly on northern village roads; stay on signposted routes.

### Samtskhe-Javakheti
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/regions/samtskhe-javakheti/
Samtskhe-Javakheti falls into two quite different halves. Samtskhe is the Mtkvari valley from Borjomi through Akhaltsikhe and on to Vardzia: pine forest, mineral water and fortresses. Javakheti is what lies above it, a volcanic plateau around 2,000 metres with lakes, wind and a horizon with almost no trees on it.

Borjomi is known for its central park and the spring where the warm mineral water is drunk straight from the source. Above the town spreads Borjomi-Kharagauli National Park, one of the largest protected areas in the country, with marked routes long enough to take several days. In Akhaltsikhe, Rabati Castle is a fully rebuilt complex where a mosque, a church and a synagogue stand inside one set of walls, and Sapara Monastery clings to a steep slope not far above.

The headline site is Vardzia: a twelfth-century cave city cut into the cliff under Queen Tamar, tunnels and cells stacked over many levels, with the church of the Dormition preserving a portrait of Tamar painted in her lifetime. Khertvisi Fortress guards the confluence of two rivers on the way there.

On the Javakheti side are Lake Paravani and Lake Tabatskuri, the Abastumani observatory, and a genuinely severe winter. The seasons split accordingly: Samtskhe works all year, the plateau realistically from June to September. Two days is the natural minimum, with a night in Borjomi or Akhaltsikhe.
Driving: The main route is easy: motorway to Gori, then through Khashuri to Borjomi and on to Akhaltsikhe. The asphalt is good and an economy car is enough. From Akhaltsikhe through Aspindza to Vardzia the road narrows but stays surfaced.

The branches are a different story. The last few kilometres up to Sapara are steep and narrow, the climb to Abastumani is a serpentine, and the track towards Lake Tabatskuri is unpaved; for all three, ground clearance is advisable. On the Javakheti plateau the weather is the main factor. Winter temperatures fall towards minus twenty, wind drifts snow across the road, and overnight ice is normal. Even in summer the nights up there are cold and fog can settle quickly.

Fuel is available in Borjomi, Akhaltsikhe and Aspindza; towards Vardzia and out on the plateau stations are sparse, so fill the tank in advance rather than counting on the next village.

### Imereti
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/regions/imereti/
Imereti is the heart of western Georgia and the region where the climate visibly changes: the air is humid, the vegetation thicker and the winter much milder than in the east. Its centre is Kutaisi, one of the oldest cities in the country and heir to the kingdom of Colchis, today a busy place of markets, the Rioni river and Bagrati Cathedral on its hill.

Ten kilometres out of town stands Gelati Monastery, founded by King David the Builder in 1106 as both a monastery and an academy, UNESCO-listed and the single most important store of Georgian mosaic and fresco painting. Small Motsameta sits nearby on a bend above the gorge, on a rock spur with a drop on three sides.

The second layer here is karst. Prometheus Cave offers long lit galleries and an underground river; Sataplia Nature Reserve combines dinosaur footprints with a cave and a glass viewing platform; Okatse Canyon is crossed by a metal walkway suspended above the gorge; Kinchkha Waterfall drops in stages down a limestone wall. North-east, near Chiatura, the Katskhi Pillar rises some forty metres with a small church on top. To the south, Sairme is a mineral water resort in the forest.

The season is long. Caves and churches work all year, while canyons and waterfalls are best from May to October, since the walkways get slippery in winter. Two days is a comfortable minimum with a night in Kutaisi, and the region fits neatly into any longer route west.
Driving: Getting into Imereti means crossing the Likhi range. The main E60 runs over the Rikoti Pass and has been rebuilt in stages with new tunnels and bridges; parts are open, and on other parts you can still meet construction detours and delays, so allow slack in the schedule rather than a precise arrival time. As far as Kutaisi and inside the city the asphalt is good and an economy car is enough.

Access roads to the sites are uneven. Gelati and Prometheus are reached on asphalt; the last stretch to Okatse is rougher; and the road to Kinchkha Waterfall is gravel that deteriorates markedly after rain, which is where ground clearance stops being optional. Morning fog is common and western Georgian rain arrives without much warning, so plan on driving slowly rather than making up time. Fuel is easy in Kutaisi, Zestaponi and Khoni, less so in the villages beyond them.

### Racha-Lechkhumi
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/regions/racha-lechkhumi/
Racha-Lechkhumi is the least populated and probably the quietest region in Georgia. Mass tourism has never arrived here, and that is exactly the point: wooded valleys, stone villages, empty roads and the Caucasus ridge closing the view to the north.

The centre is Ambrolauri, in the middle of the Khvanchkara wine zone. The Aleksandrouli vines grow on these slopes, and production is small enough that the wine behaves quite differently from Kakheti's. Just outside town stands Nikortsminda Cathedral, an eleventh-century building whose carved facade and interior painting are counted among the peaks of Georgian architecture.

Around it there is water and mountain. The Shaori and Lajanuri reservoirs lie among spruce forest; Tsageri is the lower, damper centre of Lechkhumi; and above Oni the Chanchakhi valley climbs towards Shovi, where part of the infrastructure is still being rebuilt after the debris flow of 2023 — check the current situation before going. Further on towards Ghebi lie Udziro Lake and the Buba Glacier, which are jeep and hiking country rather than sightseeing.

The season is short: roughly May to October, and for the high valleys June to September. In winter snow closes the passes and some villages are cut off for weeks. Two days is the minimum that makes sense, three is more realistic, and there is no way to see this region properly in a hurry.
Driving: Racha is far. Ambrolauri is about five hours from Tbilisi and Shovi closer to seven, so treating it as a day trip is the standard mistake. There are two approaches: from Kutaisi through Tkibuli and over the Nakerala Pass, or from Zestaponi through Sachkhere. The Tkibuli line is shorter but is a serpentine and ices up in winter.

Road quality is uneven. As far as Ambrolauri and Oni it is mostly asphalt, though narrow and full of bends, and above that gravel sections begin. Towards Ghebi, Udziro Lake and the upper valleys only a 4x4 will do. Ground clearance makes life easier everywhere in the region.

Fuel exists in Ambrolauri and Oni; above Oni there is effectively none, so fill the tank in advance. Mobile coverage drops out in the gorges. Do not drive here after dark: cattle stand on the road, edges are unlit and crash barriers are frequently missing.

### Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/regions/samegrelo-zemo-svaneti/
This administrative region joins two quite different countries. Below lies Samegrelo: warm, humid and flat, planted with tea and citrus, centred on Zugdidi and the Dadiani Palace museum, a European-style residence with a botanical garden and a collection connected to the Bonaparte family. Martvili Canyon on the Abasha river is visited by boat between limestone walls, and Nokalakevi, the Archaeopolis of Byzantine sources, preserves late antique walls and a tunnel running down to the river.

Northwards the road begins to climb at the Enguri Dam, an arch dam with the long turquoise Jvari Reservoir behind it, and within three hours it delivers you into a different climate altogether. Upper Svaneti is a high mountain province with its own language, polyphony and architecture. Mestia holds the Svaneti Museum, rich in icons and manuscripts, among stone defensive towers; above it are the Hatsvali and Tetnuldi ski areas, and a forest path leads to the Chalaadi Glacier. Ushguli, a group of four villages at 2,100 metres beneath Mount Shkhara, is UNESCO-listed. The Koruldi Lakes are reached only on foot or by jeep.

Seasonality is double. Samegrelo is accessible all year, while Svaneti is at its best from June to September, with a separate winter season for skiing. Three to four days is the minimum that makes sense, and most travellers give it more.
Driving: The first thing to accept is distance: Mestia is around 470 km from Tbilisi and eight to nine hours of driving. Doing it as a return trip in one day is not realistic, so plan a night in Zugdidi, Kutaisi or Mestia itself.

The road from Zugdidi to Mestia is asphalt and technically sound, but 130 km takes roughly three hours: continuous bends, narrow sections in the Enguri gorge, rockfall zones and livestock on the carriageway. After rain or snowmelt, stones on the road are routine rather than exceptional. In winter the road to Mestia normally stays open, but winter tyres are required and chains are worth having.

Above Mestia everything changes. The final stretch to Ushguli is gravel and needs a high-clearance vehicle; the track to the Koruldi Lakes is 4x4 only. Taking a low car onto either is not covered by rental insurance. Fuel is available in Zugdidi and Mestia and effectively nowhere in between, so fill up before the climb.

### Guria
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/regions/guria/
Guria is a small region between the Black Sea and the Meskheti range, and that contrast defines it: two hours after leaving the beach you can be at two thousand metres. The climate is subtropical and humid, and the landscape is a mixture of tea and hazelnut plantations, bamboo and dense forest.

On the coast lies Ureki, a beach of black magnetic sand which has been credited with therapeutic properties since Soviet times and remains a family holiday place. In summer it is busy, and the water is exactly as warm as at Kobuleti further south. Shekvetili, with its park and concert arena, sits a little to the north.

Inland the region quietens down. Ozurgeti is the administrative centre, and beside it stands Shemokmedi Monastery, one of the principal religious sites of Guria and once a rich repository of icons and metalwork. Nabeghlavi, in the foothills, is the village behind the mineral water of the same name.

The main mountain destination is Bakhmaro, a resort of timber houses at around two thousand metres, known for its horse races in August. Bakhmaro is strictly seasonal, roughly July to September, and can only be reached on an unpaved road.

The season is clear-cut: June to September on the coast, and an even narrower window in the mountains. One or two days is enough unless Bakhmaro is on the plan, in which case add a full day for the drive alone.
Driving: The coastal highway through Ureki and Shekvetili is good asphalt and an economy car is entirely adequate. In summer, especially at weekends, this road is busy and parking near the beaches becomes difficult — arriving early solves most of it. The roads to Ozurgeti and Shemokmedi are also surfaced and easy.

Bakhmaro is another matter. From Chokhatauri it is about forty-five kilometres of unpaved road, and it takes up to three hours: loose gravel, deep ruts, a river crossing and steep climbs. Only a 4x4 belongs here, and conditions worsen sharply after rain. In winter the road is closed altogether.

Rain in western Georgia is frequent and sudden. Visibility drops quickly and the asphalt becomes slippery under the first shower after a dry spell, so leave more space than usual. Fuel is available in Ozurgeti, Lanchkhuti and Chokhatauri, but there is nothing on the climb to Bakhmaro.

### Adjara
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/regions/adjara/
Adjara is the south-western corner of Georgia: a narrow coastal strip with mountains rising steeply behind it. It is the wettest region in the country, and its dense green is a direct result of that.

Batumi is the centre of the coast, a mixture of modern towers and older European-styled quarters, with a boulevard running some six kilometres along the shore. North of the city the Botanical Garden spreads its subtropical collection over terraces directly above the sea. To the south, close to the Turkish border, stands the Roman fortress of Gonio-Apsaros; to the north lie the long beach at Kobuleti and the ruins of Petra at Tsikhisdziri.

Turning inland gives a completely different Adjara. Makhuntseti Waterfall, with a medieval arched bridge beside it, is an hour from Batumi. Mtirala National Park — the name means "the crying one" — is one of the rainiest places in Europe, receiving up to four thousand millimetres a year. Higher again, in the Adjaristsqali valley, Khulo has a cable car, stone villages and the road towards the Goderdzi Pass.

The season splits in two. The sea works from June to September, while the city and the mountains are pleasant in spring and autumn as well, when the coast is far quieter. Two or three days is a good minimum with a base in Batumi, more if you intend to go up the valley.
Driving: The main thing to know about Adjara is that it is the wettest region in Georgia. Rain arrives in any season, often suddenly and very hard. Visibility drops within minutes, water pools across the carriageway, and on mountain sections stones and branches come down onto the road. You need more following distance and less speed here than anywhere in the east of the country.

The coastal highway towards Kobuleti and Gonio is good. The difficulty is inside Batumi: in summer central parking is scarce, there is effectively none near the boulevard, and the one-way system is confusing. Leave the car in a paid lot and walk.

Towards Upper Adjara the road is surfaced as far as Khulo, though narrow and full of bends. Above that, on the way to the Goderdzi Pass, unsurfaced sections remain and ground clearance is needed; in winter the pass is frequently impassable with snow. Fuel is easy in Batumi, Kobuleti and Keda, and rare above Khulo — see pricing if you are weighing a larger car for this leg.


## Attractions

### Batumi Boulevard and Old Town
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/batumi-boulevard-old-town/
Region: Adjara | type: town | coordinates: 41.65, 41.636 | elevation: 5 m | time needed: 6 h | from Tbilisi: 370 km / 5:30 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Batumi is the capital of Adjara and the main city on Georgia's Black Sea coast. Seeing it divides neatly into two parts that lie about ten minutes' walk apart.

The first is the Boulevard. Laid out in the 1880s, it now runs for more than seven kilometres: pebble beach on one side, avenues, cycle paths, fountains and sculptures on the other. Its most famous fixture is the moving sculpture Ali and Nino, whose two figures pass through each other every evening. Nearby stand the Alphabet Tower and the cluster of modern high-rises that has completely rewritten the city skyline over the past two decades.

The second is the old town. In the late nineteenth century Batumi was a port and a free-trade centre, and the architecture reflects that: two- and three-storey buildings with deep balconies, the Piazza square, an astronomical clock and narrow streets full of cafes.

One thing to know in advance: Adjara is the wettest region in Georgia. Batumi receives roughly two and a half thousand millimetres of rain a year, and downpours are entirely possible in July and August. A three-day visit is often interrupted by one wet day. This is not a guaranteed-sunshine resort, and it is better to plan around that than be surprised by it.
Tip: Driving in the centre in summer is inefficient: parking is expensive and often full. Leave the car at your hotel and use the boulevard on foot or by rented bicycle. Evening is the best time on the promenade, when the heat drops and the fountains run. Rain is likely in any month, so keep an umbrella or a light shell in your bag rather than in the boot. ATMs, pharmacies and cafes are everywhere, and card payment is not a problem in the centre.
Route from Tbilisi: Tbilisi to Batumi is 370 km and about five and a half hours on the best road in the country. Follow the E60 through Gori, Khashuri, the new Rikoti tunnel section, Kutaisi and Samtredia, then drop down to the coast and enter Batumi past Kobuleti. The whole route is paved and much of it is dual carriageway, so an economy car is entirely sufficient. Fuel is available everywhere along the way. On summer weekends set off early, as coastal traffic backs up from mid-morning onward.

### Batumi Botanical Garden
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/batumi-botanical-garden/
Region: Adjara | type: nature | coordinates: 41.6944, 41.7075 | elevation: 100 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 380 km / 5:45 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~15 ₾
The Batumi Botanical Garden lies north of the city on Green Cape, dropping down a hillside directly above the sea. It was founded in 1912 by the Russian botanist and geographer Andrey Krasnov and now covers more than a hundred hectares, making it one of the largest botanical collections in the region.

Its structure is unusual. The garden is divided into floristic sections, each representing a specific part of the world: East Asia, North America, Australia, the Mediterranean, the Himalayas, Mexico and Colchis are all connected by paths. Thanks to the humid subtropical climate, plants grow here that would not survive anywhere else in Georgia — bamboo groves, eucalyptus, palms and magnolias.

In practical terms:

- The site is large and steep — the full circuit takes two to three hours
- The main view opens from the upper paths across the sea and the Green Cape shoreline
- A shuttle runs between the upper and lower entrances

Spring is the best season, when the magnolias and azaleas flower, but the garden is open all year and stays green through winter. Even on a grey day the light under the canopy suits photography, which is useful given how often the Adjaran coast is overcast.
Tip: Wear comfortable shoes: the garden is on a slope with constant climbs and descents, and you will typically cover more than five kilometres. If you would rather not walk it all, enter at the upper gate, exit at the lower one and take the shuttle back. Water and a hat matter in summer, a rain shell in any season — Adjaran weather turns quickly and the paths get slippery. Cafes and toilets are at both entrances. Parking is outside the grounds and charged separately.
Route from Tbilisi: It is roughly 380 km and about five and three quarter hours from Tbilisi. Take the E60 down to Batumi, then continue north along the coast road toward Green Cape: from the city centre to the garden is only 9 km, about twenty minutes. The road is paved all the way, though the last section is narrow and winding with limited overtaking. An economy car is entirely sufficient. Fill up in Batumi. On summer days the car park fills up, so arriving early is worthwhile.

### Gonio-Apsaros Fortress
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/gonio-fortress/
Region: Adjara | type: fortress | coordinates: 41.5736, 41.5744 | elevation: 10 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 385 km / 5:50 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~15 ₾
Gonio fortress stands south of Batumi, close to the Turkish border, and is one of the best-preserved Roman military structures on Georgian territory. In antiquity it was known as Apsaros and served as an important strongpoint on the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire, garrisoned by legionary troops.

The plan is characteristically Roman: a rectangular perimeter of roughly 900 metres of wall with 18 towers. Substantial stretches survive at close to full height. The fort was later used by the Byzantines and then by the Ottomans, so building work from several eras is layered on top of one another, which the excavation trenches make visible.

Inside the walls:

- Archaeological excavations — a Roman bath house, barracks, remains of the water supply
- A small museum with coins, ceramics and other finds from the site
- A grave which local tradition associates with the Apostle Matthias

The interior courtyard is now an open grassy space, and a visit takes about an hour and a half. This is one of the places where the older history of Adjara becomes visible behind the modern facade of Batumi, and it pairs naturally with a stop at the nearby beach.
Tip: There is almost no shade inside, so midday in summer is hot and very humid — morning or early evening is much better. Bring a hat and water. Closed shoes are preferable on the grassy interior. The fortress is close to the border, so carry your passport or ID card. Park at the entrance by the roadside. Cafes, shops and an ATM are two minutes away in Gonio village, and the beach is directly across the road.
Route from Tbilisi: It is about 385 km and five hours fifty from Tbilisi. Take the E60 down to Batumi, then continue south along the coast road across the Chorokhi bridge: Batumi to Gonio is only 12 km, twenty to twenty-five minutes depending on traffic. The road is good asphalt throughout and an economy car is entirely sufficient. The fortress sits directly beside the highway and is impossible to miss. Fill up in Batumi or Gonio; you do not need to drive toward the border crossing itself.

### Makhuntseti Waterfall and Arched Bridge
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/makhuntseti-waterfall/
Region: Adjara | type: waterfall | coordinates: 41.575, 41.9006 | elevation: 180 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 395 km / 6:00 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Makhuntseti lies in the Adjaristsqali valley about 30 kilometres from Batumi and combines two sights that stand only a few hundred metres apart.

The first is the waterfall: a drop of roughly thirty metres from the cliff into a natural pool, reached by a five-minute walk from the parking area. It runs all year, but its volume varies sharply. In spring and after heavy rain it is genuinely impressive; during a dry spell in August it thins out noticeably.

The second is the arched bridge, traditionally attributed to the era of Queen Tamar and dated to the medieval period. This single-span stone bridge crosses a tributary of the Adjaristsqali and is the best known of the several dozen similar bridges surviving across Adjara. You can walk across it.

The surrounding infrastructure is well developed: restaurants serving Adjaran food, wine and chacha tastings, a zipline and small shops. This is the most popular half-day trip out of Batumi, and it often continues eastward toward Khulo and Upper Adjara, which makes it a natural first stop rather than a destination in itself.
Tip: Morning is the best time; organised groups arrive around midday and the car park fills. The rocks by the waterfall are wet and slippery, so choose shoes with grip, and note the water is cold in any season. Carry a rain shell — showers in the valley are frequent and arrive suddenly. Restaurants generally accept cards, but small kiosks will want cash. Toilets are at the parking area and in the restaurants. Allow about ninety minutes for both the waterfall and the bridge.
Route from Tbilisi: It is about 395 km and six hours from Tbilisi. First drive the E60 down to Batumi, then turn east into the Adjaristsqali valley toward Khulo: Batumi to Makhuntseti is 30 km, roughly 45 minutes. The road is paved and in good condition but narrow and winding, with limited visibility on the bends; an economy car is entirely sufficient. Fill up in Batumi, as fuel stations in the valley are sparse. The turn to the waterfall is signposted and parking sits directly at the site.

### Mtirala National Park
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/mtirala-national-park/
Region: Adjara | type: nature | coordinates: 41.6772, 41.8422 | elevation: 400 m | time needed: 4 h | from Tbilisi: 385 km / 5:50 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: may-october | entry: free
Mtirala National Park lies east of Batumi on the coastal ridge and is one of the most unusual natural areas in Georgia. The name translates literally as "the weeping one", and it is accurate: more than four thousand millimetres of rain fall here each year, which puts the park among the wettest places in Europe.

The result is Colchic relict forest — evergreen understorey, moss-covered trees, ferns and lianas. This ecosystem survives from the Tertiary period and is found almost nowhere outside western Georgia, which is why the park matters internationally rather than just locally.

What the park offers:

- A short trail to the waterfall — a roughly two-hour route past a small lake
- A zipline across the river near the visitor centre
- Longer ridge routes that require an overnight stay
- The visitor centre at Chakvistavi, with an information point and camping areas

The main warning concerns weather. Rain here is the norm, not the exception, and catching a dry day is genuinely a matter of luck. Choose your clothing for wet conditions rather than sun, and treat a clear afternoon as a bonus. In compensation, the forest is at its most striking in mist, and there are far fewer visitors than on the coast.
Tip: A waterproof jacket and shoes with real grip are essential — the paths are clay-based and slippery almost all the time. Humidity is high in summer, so insect repellent is worth carrying. Allow three to four hours and start in the morning, since storms are more likely after midday. The visitor centre has toilets and a small cafe but no ATM, so bring cash for the zipline and any fees. Mobile coverage inside the forest is weak, so agree a meeting point if you split up.
Route from Tbilisi: It is about 385 km and roughly five hours fifty from Tbilisi. Take the E60 down to the coast, turn east near Chakvi and climb toward Chakvistavi: from Batumi it is 25–30 km in total, about fifty minutes. Most of the road is paved, but the final section is narrow gravel that turns slippery after rain. That is why a higher-clearance vehicle is the sensible choice here; taking a sedan up in wet weather is not worth it. Fill up in Batumi or Chakvi before turning inland.

### Khulo Cable Car and Upper Adjara
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/khulo-cable-car-upper-adjara/
Region: Adjara | type: mountain | coordinates: 41.6444, 42.3092 | elevation: 900 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 455 km / 7:20 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: may-october | entry: ~2 ₾
Khulo is the centre of Upper Adjara, about 88 kilometres from Batumi in the upper Adjaristsqali valley. Its best-known feature is the cable car linking the town to the village of Tago: a line roughly 1,700 metres long that crosses directly above the gorge, with a ride of about ten minutes.

It is worth understanding that this is not a tourist attraction. The cable car was built in the 1980s and still functions as local transport for a village with no other short route to the district centre. The cabin is basic and the view is dramatic, with the gorge and river a couple of hundred metres below.

Beyond Khulo, Upper Adjara has several other draws:

- The Goderdzi Pass at roughly 2,025 metres, east of Khulo
- The Goderdzi petrified forest, a rare deposit of fossilised trees near the pass
- Khikhani fortress, medieval ruins on a rock outcrop
- Traditional wooden houses and arched bridges scattered through the villages

In winter the road toward Goderdzi frequently becomes difficult or closes altogether, while Khulo itself remains reachable year-round with appropriate tyres.
Tip: The cable car is simple and cheap, but its timetable follows local needs and can change, so ask on arrival rather than relying on published hours. Anyone uneasy with heights will find the crossing hard: the cabin is basic and the gorge is deep. Khulo has cafes, small guesthouses and a fuel station. If you plan to continue over the Goderdzi Pass, check the weather first and fill up in Khulo, because the next fuel is a long way further on.
Route from Tbilisi: Khulo is about 455 km and seven hours twenty from Tbilisi, with the route running via Batumi: E60 to the coast, then east into the Adjaristsqali valley — 88 km and up to two hours from Batumi. The road is mostly asphalt but narrow, full of switchbacks and damaged in places, with sections prone to landslides. A higher-clearance car is noticeably more comfortable here. If you continue over the Goderdzi Pass, a 4x4 becomes necessary outside the summer months, and the surface there is unsurfaced in stretches.

### Petra Fortress, Tsikhisdziri
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/petra-fortress/
Region: Adjara | type: fortress | coordinates: 41.7583, 41.7614 | elevation: 60 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 355 km / 5:20 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Petra fortress stands at Tsikhisdziri on a rocky headland that drops straight to the sea. It is one of those rare places where a historic monument and a coastal view occupy the same point.

The fortress was built in the sixth century under the emperor Justinian as a Byzantine strongpoint on the eastern Black Sea coast. The name Petra means "rock" in Greek and describes the site exactly. It is best known from the Lazic Wars: in the middle of the sixth century the confrontation between Byzantium and Sasanian Persia reached its climax here, and Petra changed hands several times during the campaigns.

Today you will find on the site:

- Remains of walls and towers, partly consolidated
- The foundations of a basilica on the upper part of the headland
- A view over the Black Sea and the coastline in both directions

The visit is short — an hour is entirely enough — and it fits neatly into a drive between Kobuleti and Batumi. The site is open, the infrastructure minimal, but in exchange it is almost never crowded, which is unusual for anything on this stretch of coast in summer.
Tip: Late afternoon is the best time, when the sun drops toward the sea — that is the point of the view here. The paths are stony and steep in places, so wear closed shoes; after rain the rock becomes genuinely slippery. There is very little shade and midday in summer is hot. Park in the marked area beside the main road. Cafes and shops are along the road toward Kobuleti, and the nearest ATM is in Kobuleti itself, about ten minutes away.
Route from Tbilisi: It is about 355 km and five hours twenty from Tbilisi. The whole route follows the E60: Gori, Khashuri, the Rikoti section, Kutaisi, Samtredia and then down the coast toward Kobuleti. Tsikhisdziri sits directly on the Kobuleti–Batumi road, so no detour or turning back is needed. The access is paved and an economy car is entirely sufficient. Fill up in Kobuleti or Batumi; both are ten to fifteen kilometres away, and there is a station on the main road nearby.

### Kobuleti Beach and Protected Areas
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/kobuleti/
Region: Adjara | type: beach | coordinates: 41.8206, 41.7783 | elevation: 5 m | time needed: 4 h | from Tbilisi: 345 km / 5:10 | road: paved | car: economy | season: june-september | entry: free
Kobuleti is Adjara's second resort town, roughly 25 kilometres north of Batumi. It differs from Batumi in kind rather than degree: there are no high-rises, no nightlife district and no busy centre. What there is instead is a beach several kilometres long, pine woods and a calmer, family-oriented rhythm.

The beach is fine pebble and longer than Batumi's, and a resort avenue runs the length of the shore, lined with cafes, sanatoria and family guesthouses. The season runs from June to mid-September.

A separate attraction is the Kobuleti Protected Areas — a sphagnum peat bog that is rare in Europe and recognised as a wetland of international importance. A wooden boardwalk crosses it, allowing you to see the specialised vegetation up close. This is what gives Kobuleti something beyond the beach, and it takes about an hour.

One important caveat: this coast is wet. In Kobuleti, as everywhere in Adjara, summer rain is a normal occurrence rather than an anomaly, and a week of guaranteed sunshine is not something anyone can promise you here.
Tip: June and September are the best months: the sea is warm and there are fewer people than in August. On a pebble beach, swimming shoes make a large difference to comfort. Sun protection matters even on overcast days, since humid air makes burning easy to underestimate. Park on the streets parallel to the main avenue, as central spaces are scarce in summer. ATMs, pharmacies and shops are in the centre; for the bog boardwalk bring cash and insect repellent.
Route from Tbilisi: Kobuleti is about 345 km and five hours ten from Tbilisi. The whole route runs on the E60: Gori, Khashuri, the new Rikoti section, Kutaisi, Samtredia and then down to the coast. Kobuleti sits directly on the Batumi highway and the access is paved throughout, so an economy car is entirely sufficient. Fuel is available everywhere along the way. On summer weekends traffic on the coastal stretch builds up considerably, so an early morning departure saves real time.

### Bakhmaro
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/bakhmaro/
Region: Guria | type: spa | coordinates: 41.8464, 42.3308 | elevation: 1950 m | time needed: 6 h | from Tbilisi: 355 km / 6:30 | road: gravel | car: offroad | season: june-september | entry: free
Bakhmaro is a climatic resort in the mountains of Guria, at roughly 1,950 metres. Its unusual reputation rests on the air: the Black Sea is only a few dozen kilometres away, yet the resort sits high in the alpine zone, so humid marine air mixes with dry mountain air. From the Soviet period onward people with respiratory problems were sent here to recover, and that tradition still shapes who comes.

The architecture is unlike anywhere else in Georgia. This is not a town of hotels but a scattered settlement of wooden cottages, many raised on stilts, spread across open pasture. In winter Bakhmaro is effectively empty: snow lies metres deep and the road closes. Life starts in July and finishes in early September.

Things to know:

- The season is short — realistically July and August, with late June and early September marginal
- The road is rough — the last few dozen kilometres are unsurfaced and get worse after rain
- Services are basic — a few cafes, family guesthouses, no ATM

In August the settlement hosts a traditional horse race, one of the best-known events in the region, which fills the place completely for several days. Outside that week, the appeal is quiet: meadows, mist rolling in from the sea below, and long evenings.
Tip: Plan a visit only in summer, and book accommodation in advance — in August, especially during the race week, there is essentially nothing free. Nights at 1,950 metres are cold even in midsummer, so warm clothing is genuinely necessary. There is no ATM and no pharmacy: bring cash and any medication you need. The last fuel is in Chokhatauri or Ozurgeti. Mobile coverage is patchy, so download the route for offline use before you leave the main road.
Route from Tbilisi: Bakhmaro is about 355 km and six and a half hours from Tbilisi. Take the E60 west through Khashuri, the Rikoti section, Kutaisi and Samtredia, then turn off toward Chokhatauri. The serious part begins there: roughly 50 km of mountain dirt road, steep, narrow and heavily potholed, which takes two to three hours on its own. A sedan is not an option here — a high-clearance 4x4 is required, and even then the surface demands patience. Do not set out on a rainy day, as sections turn to deep mud quickly.

### Ureki
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/ureki/
Region: Guria | type: beach | coordinates: 41.9928, 41.7822 | elevation: 5 m | time needed: 4 h | from Tbilisi: 320 km / 4:40 | road: paved | car: economy | season: june-september | entry: free
Ureki is a small resort settlement on the Guria coast with one very specific distinguishing feature: its beach sand is black and unusually rich in magnetite. That is the basis of its long-standing reputation, since the magnetic sand is popularly held to benefit the cardiovascular and musculoskeletal systems, which is a large part of why families with children come here year after year.

The practical difference from Batumi is simple. Ureki has sand rather than pebbles, and the entry into the water is gradual and shallow, which makes it comfortable for small children. Because the sand is black it heats quickly in the sun, so walking barefoot at midday is unpleasant.

What to expect:

- The village centre with small hotels, guesthouses and seasonal cafes
- Pine woods immediately behind the beach, providing the only real shade
- Neighbouring Shekvetili, with an amusement park and a large concert arena

The season runs from June to mid-September. September is often the best month: the sea is still warm and the crowds are far thinner than at the August peak. In winter the resort essentially shuts down, and most of what is open in summer simply is not there.
Tip: At the August peak Ureki gets crowded and parking in the centre becomes a genuine problem, so arrive in the morning or shift your trip to September. The black sand becomes very hot by midday, which makes beach sandals worth packing. Sun protection matters here: the only real shade is under the pines, so an umbrella helps. ATMs and shops are in the centre, though smaller cafes often take cash only. Book accommodation ahead in summer, as it fills early.
Route from Tbilisi: Ureki is about 320 km and four and a half to five hours from Tbilisi. The entire route follows the E60: Gori, Khashuri, the new Rikoti section, Kutaisi, Samtredia and then toward the coast in the direction of Batumi. Ureki sits directly on this road and the access is paved all the way, so an economy car is entirely sufficient. Fill up in Samtredia or Lanchkhuti. On summer weekends traffic toward Batumi backs up badly, so an early start makes a noticeable difference to the driving time.

### Shemokmedi Monastery
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/shemokmedi-monastery/
Region: Guria | type: monastery | coordinates: 41.9106, 42.0417 | elevation: 150 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 335 km / 5:00 | road: mostly_paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Shemokmedi Monastery stands on a hillside a few kilometres from Ozurgeti and is one of the principal religious centres of Guria. The complex consists of two churches and dates mainly from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, although the site was in use earlier.

Its historical importance is tied to the Gurieli, the princely house of Guria, for whom Shemokmedi served both as an episcopal seat and as a family burial place. Their donations built up the famous Shemokmedi treasury: chased icons, processional crosses and goldsmith work counted among the finest surviving examples of Georgian medieval art. Most of these objects are now kept in the treasury of the National Museum in Tbilisi and cannot be seen on site, which is worth knowing before you go.

What you will find here:

- Two stone churches in a single walled yard, with fragments of frescoes
- A bell tower and the surrounding enclosure walls
- A view over the Guria lowland from the monastery terrace

The visit is short — an hour is entirely enough. The monastery is active and ordinary parish life continues here without any tourist infrastructure, which is precisely what makes it quiet and unhurried compared with better-known Georgian monasteries.
Tip: This is a working monastery, so the dress code is enforced: women need a headscarf and a long skirt, men long trousers. You will not be admitted in shorts. Morning or late afternoon is better than the middle of the day, when services are often under way. Photography inside the churches is normally not allowed — ask before raising a camera. Park on the narrow area in front of the gate. There is no cafe or ATM here; the nearest are in Ozurgeti.
Route from Tbilisi: It is about 335 km and five hours from Tbilisi. Follow the E60 through Khashuri, the Rikoti section, Kutaisi and Samtredia, then turn toward Lanchkhuti and Ozurgeti. From Ozurgeti the monastery is only a few kilometres away: the approach is narrow asphalt, with the final stretch steep and broken in places. In dry weather an economy car manages it without difficulty, though take the last bends slowly. Fill up in Ozurgeti, since there are no fuel stations on the village road beyond it.

### Nabeghlavi
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/nabeghlavi/
Region: Guria | type: spa | coordinates: 41.9333, 42.2864 | elevation: 480 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 345 km / 5:30 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: may-october | entry: free
Nabeghlavi is a village in Chokhatauri municipality, in the foothills of Guria at roughly 480 metres. Its name is known across the country because of mineral water: the local spring is the source of one of Georgia's most widely sold table waters, and the bottling happens here.

The village itself is compact and unassuming — a valley, a river, forested slopes and the water plant. There are two reasons a traveller stops here. The first is the water and the mild, humid foothill climate that established the place as a modest health and recreation destination. The second is location: Nabeghlavi sits naturally on the road toward Bakhmaro and is the last point where the road surface and the services are still normal.

What you will find:

- The springs and bottling area, the main local landmark
- Valley paths for short walks through the forest
- The village centre with small shops and family guesthouses

This is not somewhere you would drive from Tbilisi specifically. It does fit logically into a Guria itinerary, though, particularly if you are continuing toward Bakhmaro or simply turning inland from the coast for an afternoon in the hills.
Tip: Late spring to autumn is the sensible window; winters here are damp and cold and the road higher up closes. A visit takes one to two hours, so pair it with another stop rather than treating it as a destination. If you are heading on to Bakhmaro, fill the tank here or in Chokhatauri — there is no fuel further up. There is no ATM in the village, so bring cash. Mobile coverage in the valley is uneven, and an offline map is useful.
Route from Tbilisi: It is about 345 km and five and a half hours from Tbilisi. Take the E60 west through Kutaisi and Samtredia, then turn off toward Chokhatauri and climb south-east into the valley from there. Chokhatauri to Nabeghlavi is roughly 20 km on mostly asphalt road, though it is narrow and broken in places with potholes. An economy car will manage in dry weather, but a higher-clearance vehicle is noticeably more comfortable on this stretch. Fill up in Chokhatauri before turning inland.

### Gelati Monastery
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/gelati-monastery/
Region: Imereti | type: monastery | coordinates: 42.2953, 42.7681 | elevation: 300 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 240 km / 3:30 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Gelati stands on a hillside eleven kilometres from Kutaisi and counts as the principal cultural centre of medieval Georgia. The monastery was founded in 1106 by David IV the Builder, the king who united the country and drove out the Seljuks. For him it was never only a religious house: an academy was established here teaching philosophy, geometry, rhetoric and astronomy, and contemporaries called it a second Jerusalem and a new Athens.

Gelati is inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, and that status remains current.

The heart of the complex is the main Church of the Virgin. In the apse is a 12th-century mosaic of the Theotokos flanked by archangels — one of the largest surviving medieval mosaics in the Caucasus. The walls carry layers of fresco painted between the 12th and 18th centuries, including portraits of Georgian kings.

What you see on site:

- the Church of the Virgin with its mosaic and multi-layered wall painting
- the churches of St George and St Nicholas
- the academy building, where the stone benches still stand
- the bell tower and the spring beneath it

David the Builder's grave lies at the southern gate. By tradition the king asked to be buried in the entrance itself, so that everyone entering would step over him — a last, deliberately humble gesture from Georgia's most powerful medieval ruler.
Tip: This is an active monastery: women need a headscarf and long skirt, men long trousers. Wraps are usually available at the gate, but bringing your own is safer. Morning or late afternoon is better for the mosaic, when sunlight reaches the apse. The churches hold deep shade and stay cool, so a jacket is useful even in summer. Park at the lot by the gate. A cafe and toilets sit at the entrance; the nearest ATM is in Kutaisi.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi take the E60 past Gori and Khashuri and through the new Rikoti tunnels to Kutaisi — 230 km, about three hours twenty. From Kutaisi head northeast and cover the last eleven kilometres to Gelati. The whole route is paved, with the final section narrow but in good condition. An economy car is entirely sufficient. Fuel and ATMs are plentiful in Kutaisi. Motsameta Monastery sits on the same road, so combining both in one outing takes almost no extra driving.

### Bagrati Cathedral and central Kutaisi
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/bagrati-cathedral/
Region: Imereti | type: town | coordinates: 42.2775, 42.7047 | elevation: 180 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 230 km / 3:20 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Bagrati Cathedral stands on Ukimerioni hill and is visible from most of Kutaisi. It was completed in 1003 under Bagrat III as the symbolic cathedral of a newly united Georgian kingdom. In 1692, during an Ottoman campaign, an explosion brought down the dome and much of the walls, and for nearly three centuries the building stood as a ruin.

Between 2009 and 2012 it was heavily rebuilt using modern materials, including new structural elements and a lift. Because of that intervention UNESCO removed Bagrati from the World Heritage List, and the cathedral is no longer inscribed — unlike Gelati, which retained its listing.

That does not make the visit pointless. The hill gives the best view over Kutaisi and the Rioni valley, and the building itself is an unusually clear illustration of the argument about how far restoration should go.

Down in the town:

- the Colchis Fountain on the central square, with enlarged copies of ancient goldwork
- the White Bridge and the Rioni embankment
- the Green Bazaar, good for Imeretian cheese, honey and spices
- the opera house and streets of 19th-century townhouses

Kutaisi is identified with the ancient kingdom of Colchis, and the legends of Aeetes and the Golden Fleece belong to this stretch of river.
Tip: You can drive all the way up to the cathedral and park at the top, but walking up from town is better: it takes about fifteen minutes and passes through the old quarters. Normal church dress rules apply inside. Sunset from the hill is worth staying for, though lighting on the path down is poor and a torch helps. Cafes, toilets and ATMs are all around the central square, roughly ten minutes below.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi it is the E60 straight to Kutaisi — 230 km and about three hours twenty. The motorway now runs through the new Rikoti tunnels, which has cut a significant amount off this drive. As you enter the city Bagrati is obvious on the hill to your right, so navigation is easy. The centre of Kutaisi has one-way streets and parking fills during the day. The entire route is paved and an economy car is fine. Fuel, service stations and ATMs are everywhere in the city.

### Prometheus Cave
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/prometheus-cave/
Region: Imereti | type: cave | coordinates: 42.3761, 42.6008 | elevation: 220 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 250 km / 3:45 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~25 ₾ (ნავი ~20 ₾ დამატებით)
Prometheus Cave lies by the village of Kumistavi near Tskaltubo and is the most spectacular karst system open to visitors in Georgia. It was only discovered in 1984 and opened to the public in 2011, which is why the infrastructure here is far better developed than at other Georgian caves.

The system contains more than twenty halls, of which six are laid out for visitors. The walking route is about 1.4 kilometres along concrete paths and bridges, past stalactites, stalagmites, petrified stone waterfalls and an underground river.

The lighting is coloured and theatrical. Whether that improves on a raw, unlit cave is a matter of taste, but the scale and the formations are genuinely impressive regardless.

Practical details:

- the temperature stays around fourteen degrees all year
- visits run as guided groups and last roughly an hour
- at the exit you can take a boat along the underground river for a separate fee
- the concrete underfoot is permanently wet

The cave combines naturally with Tskaltubo's abandoned Soviet sanatoriums and with Sataplia reserve to make a full day out of Kutaisi, and all three sit within twenty kilometres of each other.
Tip: Take a jacket without fail: it can be thirty degrees outside and fourteen inside, and an hour underground at that temperature feels long. Wear shoes with grip, because the concrete is constantly wet. Tickets are tied to group departures and in summer the wait can reach half an hour, so morning or mid-afternoon is quieter. The boat ride is paid separately and leaves you at a different exit. Cafe, toilets and parking are at the entrance.
Route from Tbilisi: Take the E60 from Tbilisi to Kutaisi, then head northwest through Tskaltubo to Kumistavi — around 250 km and three hours forty-five in total. The whole route is paved and in good condition; the last ten kilometres narrow but present no difficulty. An economy car is entirely sufficient. Fuel and ATMs are available in Kutaisi and Tskaltubo. Sataplia reserve lies in the same direction, so pairing the two in one day costs almost no extra driving.

### Sataplia Nature Reserve
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/sataplia-nature-reserve/
Region: Imereti | type: nature | coordinates: 42.3131, 42.6606 | elevation: 500 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 240 km / 3:30 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~20 ₾
Sataplia lies just nine kilometres from Kutaisi and is the oldest protected area in Georgia, granted reserve status back in 1935. The name means place of honey: wild bees nested in the cliff crevices and locals collected honey from them.

The reserve's defining discovery was made in 1933 by the naturalist Petre Chabukiani, who found dinosaur footprints preserved in the rock surface. Around two hundred prints have now been counted, dating to the Cretaceous period roughly 120 million years ago. Both herbivore and predator tracks are present, and the site is now protected under a covered pavilion.

Also on the territory:

- a karst cave with stalactites, of which about three hundred metres are open to visitors
- a glass-floored viewing platform cantilevered off the cliff, looking over Kutaisi and the Colchic forest
- the crater of an extinct volcano and short forest trails
- life-size dinosaur models, which children reliably enjoy more than the actual footprints

Sataplia operates on a completely different scale from Prometheus Cave — smaller and more modest — but it is interesting precisely because geology, palaeontology and Colchic forest sit together in one compact site. Both fit comfortably into a single day.
Tip: The glass platform is difficult for anyone with a fear of heights: the floor is fully transparent with the gorge directly below. Paths are paved but climb steadily; a pushchair is possible, though hard work. The cave is cool, around twenty degrees below the outside temperature in summer, so bring a light jacket. Come in the morning, since groups arrive together around midday. Cafe, toilets and parking are at the entrance, with the nearest ATM in Kutaisi.
Route from Tbilisi: Take the E60 from Tbilisi to Kutaisi — 230 km and about three hours twenty. From the city head northwest and cover the last nine kilometres to Sataplia; signposting is clear. The road is paved throughout and entirely comfortable for an economy car. Fuel and ATMs are plentiful in Kutaisi. Prometheus Cave lies in the same direction about fifteen kilometres further on, so combining both on one outing is the obvious plan.

### Okatse Canyon
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/okatse-canyon/
Region: Imereti | type: canyon | coordinates: 42.4525, 42.51 | elevation: 500 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 265 km / 4:00 | road: mostly_paved | car: economy | season: may-october | entry: ~20 ₾ + შატლი ~5 ₾
Okatse Canyon sits near the village of Gordi in Khoni municipality and has become one of the most visited natural sites in Imereti. The Okatse river cut a narrow, deep gorge into limestone, and a metal walkway around 780 metres long now runs along its wall, at points some 140 metres above the canyon floor. It ends in a viewing platform projecting into open air.

The thing to know before you go: this is not a drive-up viewpoint. The visitor centre is in Gordi, and the start of the walkway is a further couple of kilometres away. A shuttle covers part of that distance and the rest is on foot, through the old Dadiani forest park.

A realistic sequence looks like this:

- ticket and shuttle at the visitor centre
- a walk through the forest, with climbs and descents
- the metal walkway along the canyon wall and the viewing platform
- the same route back

Budget two and a half to three hours in total, and accept that only a modest share of that is spent on the canyon itself. The walkway is narrow and flexes slightly in wind, which makes it a demanding experience for anyone afraid of heights, though the structure is solid and fully railed.
Tip: Plan for three hours and wear proper walking shoes, because most of the visit is on foot rather than on the canyon walkway. After rain both the metal and the stone are slippery. Carry water — there is no shop along the trail. The last shuttle runs in the afternoon, so arriving after 15:00 is a gamble. Open or heeled shoes are a bad idea. Toilets and a cafe are at the visitor centre; the nearest ATM is in Khoni or Kutaisi.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi take the E60 to Kutaisi, then head northwest towards Khoni and on to Gordi — about 265 km and four hours in total. Motorway as far as Kutaisi, then ordinary asphalt, with the final ten to fifteen kilometres narrow and patchy in places, though an economy car will manage. You leave the car at the visitor centre car park and go no further by road. Fill up in Kutaisi or Khoni; there is no fuel station in Gordi itself.

### Kinchkha Waterfall
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/kinchkha-waterfall/
Region: Imereti | type: waterfall | coordinates: 42.4667, 42.47 | elevation: 600 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 275 km / 4:15 | road: gravel | car: suv | season: may-october | entry: ~15 ₾ + შატლი ~5 ₾
Kinchkha Waterfall lies above Okatse Canyon in Khoni municipality, and both belong to the same protected area. The water drops down a limestone wall in several stages; the total height reaches around a hundred metres, but it is a cascade rather than a single fall.

Seasonality defines the visit more than anything else. In spring and after heavy rain the waterfall is loud and powerful; by late August it often shrinks to a thin ribbon. If you want the dramatic version, May and June are the right months.

Getting there is its own story. The final stretch is gravel with deep ruts and becomes considerably harder after rain. For that reason a shuttle from the visitor centre is usually offered, and driving your own car all the way up is not always recommended. From the parking area, wooden stairs and a path lead down to the viewing decks.

What you get:

- views of the falls from two levels
- Colchic forest gorge and limestone walls
- the option of combining it with Okatse Canyon in one day

Both sites fit into a single day, but only if you leave Tbilisi early. Attempting Kinchkha as an afternoon add-on after a late start regularly ends with people arriving as the last shuttle leaves.
Tip: The falls are fullest in May and June and can shrink dramatically by the end of summer. The last section of road is gravel — if you are in a sedan, leave it at the visitor centre and take the shuttle up. The wooden stairs are slippery in rain, so shoes with grip are essential. Bring water and food, as there is no shop above. Toilets are only at the visitor centre, and the nearest ATM is in Khoni.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi take the E60 to Kutaisi, then head towards Khoni and Gordi — 275 km and roughly four hours fifteen. Beyond Gordi the road towards Kinchkha narrows, and the final five or six kilometres are gravel with steep pitches and washouts after rain. A sedan is a poor choice on that section; a crossover or the shuttle is much better. In winter the track is often impassable. Fill up in Kutaisi or Khoni. You can compare car categories on the /fleet/ page.

### Katskhi Pillar
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/katskhi-pillar/
Region: Imereti | type: monastery | coordinates: 42.2919, 43.2242 | elevation: 500 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 205 km / 3:00 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Katskhi Pillar stands near Chiatura by the village of Katskhi: a natural limestone monolith rising roughly forty metres from the surrounding land, ending in a flat summit. On top sit a small church and monastic cells, traditionally dated to the 9th or 10th century.

The site was a place of worship in pagan times, and later the tradition of stylites — monks who lived on pillars — took hold here. Its modern history began in the 1990s, when the monk Maxime Qavtaradze climbed up and lived there in near-total isolation for decades, hauling food and building material up on a chain ladder and a winch.

Important: visitors are not allowed to climb the pillar. The ladder is reserved for clergy, tourists are not permitted to the top, and no exceptions are made. What remains is the view from below, which is genuinely enough: a forty-metre stone column crowned by a church is striking from a distance.

At the base is a monastery complex with a church and courtyard, open to visitors. A stop takes about forty minutes, and it combines well with the cable cars and Soviet mining landscape of Chiatura a short drive away.
Tip: Do not plan on going up — you cannot even approach the ladder, and this is enforced. The best photographs come in the morning or late afternoon, when the sun hits the pillar from the side; at midday the light is flat. Standard monastery dress applies in the lower courtyard: headscarf for women, long trousers for men. Forty minutes covers it. Toilets are basic; cafes and ATMs are in Chiatura, about ten kilometres away.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi take the E60 west towards Zestaponi, then turn north for Chiatura and continue about ten kilometres to Katskhi — around 205 km and three hours. The route is paved throughout. The Chiatura road is narrow and damaged in places by mining traffic, but it presents no problem for an economy car. Fuel is available in Zestaponi and Chiatura. There is a small parking area by the pillar with limited space for coaches.

### Motsameta Monastery
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/motsameta-monastery/
Region: Imereti | type: monastery | coordinates: 42.2825, 42.7444 | elevation: 250 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 235 km / 3:25 | road: mostly_paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Motsameta stands six kilometres from Kutaisi on a narrow rock spur above the gorge of the Tskaltsitela river. In scale it cannot compete with Gelati, but its setting is far more dramatic: from the edge of the courtyard the gorge drops away almost vertically.

The name means the martyrs. During the Arab invasions of the 8th century the brothers David and Constantine Mkheidze were tortured to death here for refusing to renounce their faith. Tradition says their bodies were thrown into the river and the water ran red, which is where the river's name — Tskaltsitela, red water — is said to come from.

Today the brothers' relics rest in a wooden casket inside the church. An old custom survives here: pilgrims pass under the casket three times and make a wish. The ritual is still very much alive, and it is what most visitors stop for.

The visit is short, around forty minutes. The church is small and the courtyard modest, but the view and the quiet make it a natural continuation after Gelati. Both sit on the same road out of Kutaisi, so one outing covers them.
Tip: This is a working monastery: women need a headscarf and long skirt, men long trousers, and wraps are usually available at the gate. The courtyard edge is unfenced above a steep gorge, so keep children close. Come after Gelati, in the second half of the day, once the coaches have moved on. Park at the small area before the final bend. Toilets are basic; the nearest cafe and ATM are back in Kutaisi.
Route from Tbilisi: Take the E60 from Tbilisi to Kutaisi — 230 km and about three hours twenty. From the city follow the same road as for Gelati, then after roughly five kilometres turn right for Motsameta. The final two kilometres are narrow, steep and winding asphalt where two cars barely pass and coaches cause real congestion. An economy car manages it, but take care in the wet. Fill up and draw cash in Kutaisi, as there is nothing along the way.

### Sairme Resort
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/sairme-resort/
Region: Imereti | type: spa | coordinates: 41.8992, 42.7397 | elevation: 950 m | time needed: 4 h | from Tbilisi: 255 km / 4:00 | road: paved | car: economy | season: may-october | entry: free (წყარო)
Sairme lies in Baghdati municipality, in a narrow, densely wooded gorge at roughly 950 metres above sea level. It took shape as a resort in the Soviet period and was comprehensively rebuilt during the 2010s; today it has modern hotels, treatment buildings and a tidy promenade.

The reason people come is the mineral springs. Their composition and mineralisation differ from one another, and each has traditionally been used for different conditions — digestion, kidneys, metabolism. The water is drawn directly in the drinking pavilions and tasting it costs nothing.

Beyond the drinking cure:

- forest walking trails along the gorge, from short loops to half-day routes
- spa and bath treatments at the hotels
- short drives towards Baghdati and Vani for a change of scene

Sairme stays cool even in summer. The gorge is tight, the forest dense, and daytime temperatures run several degrees below Kutaisi, which is exactly why Georgians use it to escape August heat. This is not a one-hour stop: either give it half a day or stay the night. Arriving, drinking a glass of water and driving away misses the point of the place entirely.
Tip: If you want an actual treatment course, check with a hotel in advance — procedures are booked and charged separately, while simply tasting the water at the pavilions is free. Bring an empty bottle. Evenings in the gorge are chilly and a jacket is useful even in summer. Walking shoes matter for the trails. Cafes and shops are on the resort itself, but ATMs are in Baghdati and Kutaisi, so draw cash before you arrive.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi take the E60 towards Kutaisi, then turn south for Baghdati and continue about twenty kilometres up the gorge — roughly 255 km and four hours in total. The road is paved the whole way and has been resurfaced in recent years, but it is narrow and winding, and in winter the gorge collects ice and snow. An economy car is sufficient; a crossover is more comfortable in the cold months. Fill up in Kutaisi or Baghdati before the climb.

### Sighnaghi
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/sighnaghi/
Region: Kakheti | type: town | coordinates: 41.6197, 45.9214 | elevation: 790 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 110 km / 1:50 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Sighnaghi stands on a ridge some four hundred metres above the floor of the Alazani Valley, and that position is the whole point of the place. From any eastern edge of town the ground drops away and a flat green plain runs out to the wall of the Greater Caucasus — on a clear day the snow line is sharp enough to trace with a finger. The town itself is tiny, well under two thousand residents, and was rebuilt in the mid-2000s with red-tiled roofs, carved wooden balconies and cobbled lanes. Some travellers find the restoration a little too tidy; most simply enjoy it.

The serious monument here is the fortress wall. King Erekle II had it built in the 1770s as a refuge for the surrounding villages during raids from the north-east. Roughly four kilometres of curtain wall survive along with twenty-three towers, which makes it one of the most complete defensive circuits in Georgia. Two sections are open: stairways lead up onto the rampart, and the tower walks give a far better panorama than street level does.

On the main square, the Sighnaghi Museum holds regional archaeology downstairs and a room of Niko Pirosmani canvases upstairs — the painter was born nearby at Mirzaani. Around the square are wine bars and family cellars pouring qvevri wine by the glass, plus the small marriage house that earned the town its "city of love" nickname.
Tip: Arrive in the afternoon and stay for sunset — the Alazani view is at its best when the last light hits the Caucasus. Park below the main square or along Chavchavadze Street; the centre is small enough to cross on foot in minutes. Three hours covers the square, the museum and one stretch of wall, but climbing the towers takes longer and the steps are uneven, so wear proper shoes. Cafés, ATMs and toilets are all on or beside the square.
Route from Tbilisi: Leave Tbilisi on the Kakheti Highway through Sagarejo and Badiauri, carry on past Tsnori, then take the signed left turn and climb — about 110 km and one hour fifty in total. The surface is asphalt the whole way and an economy car is entirely adequate, though the final ascent is a narrow series of switchbacks. Fuel is easy in Sagarejo, Gurjaani and Tsnori. You can return over the Gombori Pass via Telavi for a more scenic drive; it costs roughly half an hour more and closes in heavy snow.

### Bodbe Monastery
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/bodbe-monastery/
Region: Kakheti | type: monastery | coordinates: 41.5992, 45.9294 | elevation: 710 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 112 km / 1:55 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Bodbe lies barely two kilometres from Sighnaghi, so the two fit naturally into one outing. The monastery was built over the grave of St Nino, the woman credited with converting Georgia to Christianity in the fourth century; tradition places her burial precisely here. The first church is attributed to King Mirian, while the three-nave basilica standing today is largely ninth-century, reworked several times, with a bell tower added in the nineteenth.

The grounds are calm and carefully kept. A cypress avenue runs from the gate to the church, a rose garden sits alongside it, and the terrace at the far end opens onto a wide view over the Alazani Valley. Inside the basilica, St Nino's tomb occupies the right-hand nave and the walls keep their nineteenth-century painting. This is a working convent, so the atmosphere is quiet and photography inside the church is restricted.

Many pilgrims continue down a footpath below the monastery to St Nino's Spring. The descent takes around twenty minutes; the climb back is noticeably harder on a hot day, since the trail is steep with little shade. At the bottom there is a small chapel and a pool where visitors may immerse themselves — if you intend to, bring your own shirt and towel, as nothing is provided.
Tip: A dress code applies: women need a long skirt and a head covering, men long trousers. Wraps are usually available at the entrance, but bringing your own scarf saves waiting. Come early in the morning or later in the afternoon; midday brings a steady flow of tour coaches. Parking sits right at the gate and is free. Two hours covers the church, the garden and the viewpoint; adding the spring costs another hour and needs decent footwear.
Route from Tbilisi: The drive is the same as for Sighnaghi: the Kakheti Highway through Sagarejo, Badiauri and on past Tsnori, roughly 112 km and just under two hours. The Bodbe turning comes shortly before Sighnaghi itself and is clearly signposted; the last two kilometres are a narrow but properly surfaced lane. An economy car is fine throughout. Fill up in Tsnori or Gurjaani, where stations are frequent. Sighnaghi is five minutes further on, so almost everyone combines the two in a single trip.

### Telavi and Batonis Tsikhe
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/telavi-batonis-tsikhe/
Region: Kakheti | type: town | coordinates: 41.9192, 45.4731 | elevation: 755 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 95 km / 1:45 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~7 ₾
Telavi is the administrative and practical centre of Kakheti — the market, the hospital, the banks and by far the widest choice of accommodation in the region are all here. The town is built in terraces on the slope of the Tsiv-Gombori range, and from the main avenue the Alazani Valley and the Caucasus wall open out directly ahead. This is the natural base from which Alaverdi, Ikalto, Tsinandali and Gremi can all be reached in a single day.

In the centre stands Batonis Tsikhe, the royal residence of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries: Erekle II's palace, two small court churches, a bathhouse and the enclosing wall. The complex has been restored and works as a museum, with a historical exhibition, the royal rooms and a walk around the courtyard perimeter. In front of it is the well-known equestrian statue of Erekle II, and the terrace beside it gives the town's best panorama.

A short walk away, in its own small enclosure, stands the Telavi plane tree — an oriental plane estimated at around nine hundred years old, with a trunk some eleven metres around. The town market, five minutes from the castle, is worth a stop in its own right: churchkhela, Telavi cheese, fruit, and local wine sold by the bottle or straight from plastic canisters.
Tip: Telavi makes a sensible overnight base if you are giving Kakheti two days; room rates here run below Sighnaghi. The ticket at Batonis Tsikhe covers the museum, while walking into the courtyard is normally free. Leave the car near the Erekle statue, where parking costs nothing. Three hours covers the castle, the plane tree and the market. Cafés and ATMs line the central avenue, but bring cash for the market itself.
Route from Tbilisi: The quickest route is over the Gombori Pass: out of Tbilisi via Vaziani, Ujarma and Gombori, about 95 km and an hour and three quarters. The road is asphalt but narrow and winding at the top, and it can close briefly after heavy winter snowfall. The alternative is the Kakheti Highway through Sagarejo and Gurjaani — 120 km and over two hours, but flat and untroubled. An economy car is adequate on either. Fuel up in Sagarejo or in Telavi itself, where several stations sit on the approach road.

### Alaverdi Cathedral
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/alaverdi-cathedral/
Region: Kakheti | type: monastery | coordinates: 42.0311, 45.3772 | elevation: 470 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 110 km / 2:05 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Alaverdi stands in the middle of the Alazani plain, some twenty kilometres north-west of Telavi. The cathedral was raised in the early eleventh century under the Kakhetian king Kvirike III and remained the tallest building in Georgia for close to nine hundred years, its dome reaching about fifty metres. The figure reads dryly on paper, but the effect on the ground is considerable: on flat farmland, above villages and vineyards, the church is visible from a long way off and gives the whole valley its scale.

The monastery is older than the cathedral. It was founded in the sixth century by Joseph of Alaverdi, one of the Assyrian Fathers, and his tomb is still inside the church. The interior is almost bare, and that is exactly the point — a tall, narrow volume, light falling from high windows, and fragments of wall painting, some of it dating to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. The acoustics are unusually good, and a service here is worth timing your visit around.

A defensive wall of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries encloses the cathedral together with a refectory, a bathhouse and burial vaults. The monastery keeps its own cellar, and Alaverdi wine — made by the monks in buried qvevri — is among the better-known labels of the region. The Alaverdoba feast in September fills the grounds.
Tip: The dress code is enforced: women need a long skirt and head covering, men long trousers, and shorts will not get you through the gate. Wraps hang by the entrance. Morning is the best time, with light coming through the eastern windows and the tour traffic not yet arrived. Parking is on the free forecourt outside the wall. An hour is genuinely enough. There is a toilet on site; the nearest café is in the neighbouring village.
