Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi take the Gombori Pass road to Telavi (95 km), then continue north-west towards Akhmeta for another fifteen kilometres or so — about 110 km and two hours in total. Once on the plain the road is flat, well-surfaced asphalt and an economy car is entirely adequate; the turning is clearly visible and the last kilometre is a narrow but paved village street. Fill up in Telavi. If Gombori is shut by snow, use the Sagarejo–Gurjaani highway instead, which adds roughly thirty kilometres.

### Gremi
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/gremi/
Region: Kakheti | type: fortress | coordinates: 41.9772, 45.6944 | elevation: 470 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 125 km / 2:20 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~5 ₾
In the sixteenth century Gremi was the capital of the Kingdom of Kakheti: a trading town of several thousand people on a branch of the Silk Road, with Armenian, Persian and Georgian quarters, workshops, a caravanserai and a royal palace. In 1615 the campaign of Shah Abbas I destroyed it completely — the population was killed or deported to Persia, and the capital moved to Telavi. What survives today is the citadel on its hill; the town itself is under the fields below.

The centrepiece is the Church of the Archangels, built in 1565 under King Levan: an elongated brick church with a tall drum and dome, one of the clearest examples of Kakhetian architecture absorbing Persian influence. Inside, substantial fragments of sixteenth-century painting remain, including donor portraits. Beside it stands the bell tower, whose three floors now house a small museum of finds from the site.

The climb up to the citadel takes five minutes and repays it with a wide view over the Alazani plain, its vineyards, and the Caucasus ridge beyond. The complex is compact — an hour covers it comfortably — which makes it a natural stop on a day that also takes in Nekresi and Kvareli. Archaeological excavation of the lower town continues in the fields at the foot of the hill.
Tip: An hour is enough, including the tower. The ticket is nominal and covers the tower museum; walking into the grounds is free. Park at the entrance directly off the road. Morning or late afternoon gives the best light — there is almost no shade on the hill and summer middays are hot. Modest dress is expected inside the church, so avoid shorts and bare shoulders. There is a toilet on site; the nearest cafés are in Kvareli.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi cross the Gombori Pass to Telavi, then continue north-east towards Kvareli for another thirty kilometres or so — around 125 km and two hours twenty in total. The road is asphalt throughout and an economy car is entirely sufficient; Gremi sits directly beside the main road, so there is no turning to hunt for. Fuel is available in Telavi and Kvareli. The alternative route via Sagarejo and Gurjaani is flatter but roughly thirty kilometres longer.

### Ikalto Academy
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/ikalto-academy/
Region: Kakheti | type: monastery | coordinates: 41.9744, 45.3608 | elevation: 620 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 100 km / 1:55 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Ikalto lies about ten kilometres west of Telavi on the slope of the Tsiv-Gombori range, in a shaded yard of cypresses and plane trees. The monastery was founded in the sixth century by Zenon of Ikalto, one of the Assyrian Fathers, and his tomb is in the main church. Three churches stand on the grounds: the Church of the Holy Spirit, dated to the eighth or ninth century, and the smaller Trinity and Kvirike churches beside it.

What made the name, though, was the academy. In the early twelfth century, under David the Builder, Arsen of Ikalto established a school here that ranked alongside Gelati as one of the two leading centres of learning of the age. Students were taught theology, philosophy and rhetoric, but also practical crafts — winemaking, smithing, pottery. Tradition holds that Shota Rustaveli studied here; there is no documentary proof, but the association is old and firmly held.

The academy building was burned during Shah Abbas's campaign in 1616, and what remains is the shell of its walls: arches, window openings, the working rooms at one end. In the yard you can see qvevri sunk into the ground, evidence that wine was made on site. The place is quiet and shaded, with a fraction of the visitor traffic that Alaverdi gets, and that alone makes it a rewarding stop.
Tip: Ikalto pairs naturally with Alaverdi — both are half an hour from Telavi and fit into one morning. An hour on site is enough. Modest dress is expected in the churches and head coverings are laid out at the door. Park in front of the yard, in the shade of the trees. Entry is free, though small change is useful for candles. Cafés and ATMs are only in Telavi; there is a toilet on the grounds.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi cross the Gombori Pass to Telavi (95 km), then take the Akhmeta road west for around five kilometres and turn left towards the village of Ikalto — roughly 100 km and just under two hours in total. The whole route is asphalt; the final two kilometres are a narrow village street climbing gently uphill. An economy car handles it without difficulty. Fill up in Telavi. In winter, if Gombori is closed by snow, use the flat Sagarejo–Gurjaani road instead.

### Nekresi Monastery
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/nekresi-monastery/
Region: Kakheti | type: monastery | coordinates: 41.96, 45.7783 | elevation: 600 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 135 km / 2:25 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~3 ₾
Nekresi sits on the southern slope of the Caucasus near Kvareli, about three hundred metres above the valley floor. The complex holds several buildings, and the oldest of them is a small three-nave chapel dated to the second half of the fourth century — one of the earliest surviving church structures in the country, built within a few decades of Christianity becoming the state religion. It is plain, low and easy to walk past, which is part of its appeal.

Beside it stand the Trinity church of the sixth or seventh century, a ninth-century archbishop's palace with a vaulted hall, and a large marani where some fifty qvevri are sunk into the floor. The monastery was renewed in the sixth century by Abibos of Nekresi, one of the Assyrian Fathers, whose name is tied to the struggle against Zoroastrian fire worship and who was killed for it.

Private cars cannot drive up. You leave the car at a lower car park and take a shuttle minibus that covers the two kilometres of steep climbing; alternatively you can walk the path in about forty minutes. From the top the Alazani plain and the Caucasus wall open out across the whole horizon, and for many visitors that panorama, rather than any single building, is what the trip is remembered for. The grounds are shaded and stay pleasant even in summer.
Tip: Plan around the shuttle. Tickets are sold at the lower car park, minibuses run every few minutes, but the last descent is fairly early in the evening, so do not arrive at the end of the day. Two hours covers the ride up, the complex and the viewpoint. Dress modestly; wraps are available on site. The lower car park has a toilet and a small kiosk, but the nearest ATM is in Kvareli, so carry cash.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi cross the Gombori Pass to Telavi, then head towards Kvareli past Gremi — around 135 km and roughly two and a half hours. The entire route is asphalt and an economy car is sufficient, since the steep section is handled by the shuttle. The turning for Nekresi is on the left off the main road and is signposted. Fuel is available in Telavi and Kvareli. The flat alternative is the Kakheti Highway via Sagarejo and Gurjaani, about thirty kilometres longer but with no mountain pass.

### Tsinandali Estate
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/tsinandali-estate/
Region: Kakheti | type: museum | coordinates: 41.8917, 45.5717 | elevation: 560 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 100 km / 1:55 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~15 ₾
Tsinandali lies eight kilometres from Telavi on the Kvareli road and is the most polished museum complex in Kakheti. The estate belonged to Alexander Chavchavadze, a founding figure of Georgian romanticism who was raised in St Petersburg and poured the European taste he brought back into the design of his property. The house dates from the first half of the nineteenth century, and the interiors have been restored with period furniture, family portraits and the library.

Behind the house lies a twelve-hectare ornamental park in which Chavchavadze planted species brought from Europe and the Near East. The paths, lawns and the long view over the Alazani Valley survive, and it was here that the estate held the receptions that drew visitors as far afield as Alexandre Dumas, who wrote about his stay.

The cellar deserves separate attention. In 1835 Chavchavadze set up the first European-style wine production in Georgia here — ageing in oak barrels and bottling, instead of the traditional qvevri. The cellar's library still holds bottles from the nineteenth century, and the estate lent its name to the dry white Tsinandali blend of Rkatsiteli and Mtsvane. A ticket normally covers the house and park, with tastings priced separately; in summer the park hosts a classical music festival.
Tip: Tsinandali works well in the middle of the day, when you want a break from churches — there is shade, benches and a café in the park. The standard ticket covers house and park; a park-only ticket is cheaper. If you plan to taste, decide in advance who drives: the drink-driving limit in Georgia is very strict and checks are frequent. Parking at the entrance is free. Two hours is enough, and there are toilets and an ATM on site.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi cross the Gombori Pass to Telavi (95 km), then continue eight kilometres towards Kvareli — about 100 km and just under two hours in total. The estate sits directly on the road with a large car park and a signed entrance. The whole route is asphalt and an economy car is entirely adequate. Fill up in Telavi. In winter, if Gombori closes, take the Kakheti Highway through Sagarejo and Gurjaani instead, which adds roughly twenty-five kilometres.

### Kvareli and the Kindzmarauli zone
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/kvareli-kindzmarauli/
Region: Kakheti | type: winery | coordinates: 41.9497, 45.8125 | elevation: 450 m | time needed: 4 h | from Tbilisi: 145 km / 2:30 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~25 ₾
Kvareli sits at the northern edge of the Alazani Valley, right against the slopes of the Caucasus, and that position defines its wine. The protected Kindzmarauli microzone spreads around the town: Saperavi grown here on stony, well-drained soil goes into the semi-sweet red that is Georgia's single most recognised label abroad. The same zone also produces dry Saperavi, which many visitors end up finding more interesting than the sweet version.

The town's headline attraction is its tunnel cellars. Kilometres of galleries cut into the rock in the Soviet period now serve as wine storage: a constant temperature year-round, bottles racked into the walls on both sides, and tasting halls at the far end. A tour usually runs about an hour and a half and includes tasting. Beyond the large producers, the surrounding villages hold dozens of family cellars where the owner pours qvevri wine straight from his own vessels.

Kvareli also has two lakes. Kvareli Lake lies five kilometres above the town on the slope, with a hotel, a beach and a view across the whole valley; the smaller Ilia Lake is close to the centre. Both fill up in summer, though on a hot Kakhetian afternoon spending time beside water is probably the most sensible plan available.
Tip: Treat Kvareli as an overnight stop rather than a drive-through — getting back behind the wheel after a tasting is not worth it. Georgia's drink-driving limit is very strict and roadside checks are common, so either stay the night or agree on a designated driver in advance. Book cellar tours ahead, especially in September and October during the harvest. ATMs and shops are in the centre; at the lake there are only cafés and hotel restaurants.
Route from Tbilisi: Two options. Over the Gombori Pass via Telavi and Gremi is about 145 km and a little over two and a half hours. Alternatively take the Kakheti Highway through Sagarejo, Gurjaani and Akhalsopeli — a similar distance, flat and reliable in winter when the pass may close. Both are asphalt end to end and an economy car is entirely sufficient. Fuel is available in Telavi, Gurjaani and Kvareli itself. The final five kilometres up to the lake are a paved but steady climb.

### David Gareja
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/david-gareja/
Region: Kakheti | type: monastery | coordinates: 41.4472, 45.3778 | elevation: 830 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 75 km / 1:50 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: all | entry: free
David Gareja lies south-east of Tbilisi on the Gareja ridge and looks nothing like the rest of Kakheti. Instead of vineyards and forest there is semi-desert: treeless, rolling, green for a few weeks in spring and a bleached yellow-grey for the rest of the year. The complex was founded in the sixth century by David Garejeli, one of the Assyrian Fathers, and grew over the centuries into dozens of separate monastic units scattered along the ridge.

The main and most accessible is the Lavra — a working monastery of terraced courtyards, cells cut into the rock face, a bell tower and David's tomb. From the Lavra a path climbs to the crest of the ridge and drops down the far side to the Udabno complex, where cave walls keep frescoes of the eleventh to thirteenth centuries. The round trip up and back takes roughly an hour and a half over steep, loose ground.

The landscape here is the attraction in its own right. From the crest an apparently endless steppe opens out, covered in flowers in April and May; tortoises, snakes and birds of prey are common sights. Spring is by far the best season — mild and green. A summer midday is hard going: there is effectively no shade and temperatures reach the high thirties.
Tip: Part of the complex runs along a disputed section of the border, and the climb up to the Udabno caves is periodically closed. This is routine rather than dramatic — ask at the Lavra gate when you arrive and you will be told the current situation; the Lavra itself is almost always open. Bring water, a hat and sun protection, since there is no shade anywhere on the ridge, and dress modestly for the monastery. The nearest café, ATM and toilet are back in Udabno village.
Route from Tbilisi: Leave Tbilisi either via Rustavi or via Sagarejo, then follow signs towards the village of Udabno — about 75 km and one hour fifty in total. Most of the route is paved, but the final stretch is rough and develops potholes after winter. In dry weather an economy car will get through; a crossover with higher ground clearance is far more comfortable and genuinely advisable after rain. The last dependable fuel is in Sagarejo — the following fifty kilometres are close to empty, so fill the tank before you turn off.

### Lagodekhi Protected Areas
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/lagodekhi-protected-areas/
Region: Kakheti | type: nature | coordinates: 41.8272, 46.2792 | elevation: 450 m | time needed: 6 h | from Tbilisi: 160 km / 2:40 | road: paved | car: economy | season: may-october | entry: free
Lagodekhi was established in 1912 and is the oldest protected area in Georgia. It runs up the southern slope of the Caucasus from the floor of the Alazani Valley to peaks above three thousand metres, and that range of altitude is what gives it its variety: hornbeam and beech forest low down, subalpine meadow higher, then rock and scree at the top. Chamois, bezoar goat, brown bear and red deer all live inside the reserve.

Most routes start from a single base, the visitor centre in Lagodekhi town. The short option is the Gurgeniani waterfall, three to four hours there and back on a well-marked forest path that stays cool even in summer. A step up are the Mashavera falls and the nine-kilometre circular forest trail, both comfortable half-day walks with a solid climb in the middle.

The reserve's headline objective is Black Rock Lake, a glacial lake at around 2,800 metres directly on the Azerbaijani border. The trek takes two or three days with a night at a bivouac site or shelter, and runs from June to October; snow lingers well into May. Registration at the visitor centre is compulsory for every walk, and because the upper route enters a border zone, you must carry your passport for the multi-day trek.
Tip: Start at the visitor centre — registration is free and mandatory, and you get a map plus current trail conditions at the same time. Leave the car there. For a day walk, trainers and two litres of water are enough; you will not be sent up to Black Rock Lake without a tent and a passport. Ticks are present in the forest, so covered clothing is sensible. Cafés and ATMs are in the centre of Lagodekhi town.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi take the Kakheti Highway through Sagarejo, Badiauri, Tsnori and Kvareli, then continue east to Lagodekhi — about 160 km and two hours forty. The road is asphalt the whole way and has improved considerably in recent years, so an economy car is entirely adequate. The visitor centre is signposted at the northern edge of town. Fuel and shops are available in Lagodekhi itself. Note that crossing into Azerbaijan is not permitted in a Georgian rental car.

### Omalo and Tusheti
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/omalo-tusheti/
Region: Kakheti | type: mountain | coordinates: 42.3742, 45.6392 | elevation: 1880 m | time needed: 8 h | from Tbilisi: 220 km / 6:30 | road: 4x4_only | car: offroad | season: june-september | entry: free
Tusheti lies north of the main ridge of the Caucasus, and the only way in is over the Abano Pass at 2,850 metres: seventy kilometres of gravel from Pshaveli to Omalo, narrow the whole way, cut into the slope, with no barriers. The road appears regularly on lists of the world's most dangerous drives, and it earns the reputation honestly. This is the single hardest constraint of any trip in Georgia and it dictates everything else about the visit.

Omalo is the regional centre. Lower Omalo is the village with guesthouses and a shop; Upper Omalo sits on the hill above it around a cluster of Tushetian defensive towers that has become the visual signature of the region. Trails run out from here to Diklo, Shenako, Dartlo and Chesho, villages a few hours apart on foot that form the classic multi-day trekking circuit.

The road normally opens in early June and closes at the end of October. In winter Tusheti empties almost completely — a few dozen people stay, reachable only by helicopter. The summer window is therefore short, and weather on the pass can turn within a couple of hours. Mobile coverage and internet are patchy, and there is no ATM anywhere in the region.
Tip: This is not an ordinary day out. You need a genuine high-clearance 4x4 and a driver comfortable with exposed gravel, and you must confirm in advance whether your rental agreement permits the Abano Pass — many companies explicitly exclude it; see our /terms/. Plan at least two nights, since a day trip makes no sense. Carry cash, spare fuel, warm layers and your own medication: even the pharmacy in Omalo is minimal, and the nearest hospital is hours away.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi to Akhmeta and on to Pshaveli the road is asphalt — about 150 km covered in two and a half hours. At Pshaveli the real section begins: seventy kilometres of gravel over the Abano Pass, which realistically takes four hours or more. That gives 220 km and around six and a half hours in total without stops. The last fuel station is in Akhmeta; there is none between there and Omalo, so start with a full tank. After rain the surface deteriorates sharply and landslides are common.

### Birtvisi
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/birtvisi-fortress/
Region: Kvemo Kartli | type: fortress | coordinates: 41.6472, 44.5586 | elevation: 900 m | time needed: 4 h | from Tbilisi: 55 km / 1:20 | road: gravel | car: suv | season: may-october | entry: free
Birtvisi is the strangest piece of terrain in Kvemo Kartli: a massif of limestone that erosion has broken into narrow gorges, freestanding towers and natural gateways. The whole area covers only a few square kilometres, yet orientation inside it is genuinely difficult — the paths wind between rock walls, sightlines close down to a few metres, and people regularly lose track of the way they came in.

In the Middle Ages this natural relief made a fortress. Birtvisi is mentioned from the eleventh century and was considered impregnable: its walls simply linked existing cliffs, so very little construction was needed to hold it. Timur took it in 1403, an event unusual enough that the chronicles of his campaign singled it out. What survives today are fragments of curtain wall and the tower known as Sveti, the "Pillar", perched on a rock spire and visible from a distance.

Birtvisi is a hiking destination rather than a monument to be looked at. The standard route takes three to five hours and includes squeezing through slot gorges, walking a small stream bed and short but steep scrambles. Waymarking is poor, and groups without a guide or a downloaded GPS track routinely take wrong turnings.
Tip: Skip Birtvisi during and just after rain: the limestone turns slippery and water rises in the gorges. You need proper hiking shoes, long trousers, two litres of water and a charged phone with an offline map, since some sections require using your hands. Park for free in the last village. There is no infrastructure at all — no café, no toilet, no ATM and no reliable phone signal inside the canyon — so carry everything you will need.
Route from Tbilisi: Leave Tbilisi on the Rustavi road, then head towards Tetritskaro and the village of Tbisi — roughly 55 km and an hour and twenty. Most of it is paved, but the last five kilometres or so are gravel, rutted and rough even in dry weather. An economy car is not advisable here; a crossover with real ground clearance is much safer, and after rain the track can become impassable in a low car. The final fuel station and shop are in Tetritskaro, so stock up before turning off.

### Dmanisi
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/dmanisi/
Region: Kvemo Kartli | type: archaeology | coordinates: 41.3311, 44.3439 | elevation: 910 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 85 km / 1:50 | road: mostly_paved | car: economy | season: may-october | entry: ~15 ₾
Dmanisi holds two entirely different histories on the same promontory above the confluence of the Mashavera and Pinezauri rivers. The first is medieval: a town and citadel that served as a significant trading node between the eleventh and fourteenth centuries. What remains is the defensive wall, a bathhouse, burial vaults and Dmanisi Sioni, a sixth-century basilica to which a finely carved porch was added in the thirteenth.

The second history is far deeper. From 1991, digging beneath the medieval layers, archaeologists recovered hominin remains dated to roughly 1.8 million years. These are still the oldest human ancestors found anywhere outside Africa, and the finds are often assigned their own designation, Homo erectus georgicus. Five skulls have come out of the site, including the two known in Georgia as Zezva and Mzia, along with stone tools and the bones of the animals they were used on.

There is a museum on site and a covered shelter over the excavation, where a section of the dig is left open in its original state so you can see the stratigraphy directly. The original skulls are in the Georgian National Museum in Tbilisi; Dmanisi displays casts with detailed explanation. Excavation continues each summer and visitors can often watch the work in progress.
Tip: Dmanisi rewards interest more than it rewards a casual stop — see the National Museum exhibition in Tbilisi first and the site itself will make far more sense afterwards. Two hours covers the museum and the medieval town. The ground is open with little shade, so bring a hat and water. Parking is at the entrance. Cafés and ATMs are only in Dmanisi town, about twenty kilometres from the site, so eat before or after.
Route from Tbilisi: Leave Tbilisi towards Marneuli, then turn west through Bolnisi and Kazreti to Dmanisi — around 85 km and an hour and fifty in total. The road is wide and good as far as Marneuli, then narrows, but stays paved almost the whole way. The final couple of kilometres to the site are rough, though an ordinary car gets through in dry weather. Fuel is available in Marneuli and Bolnisi. If you also plan Birtvisi, both fit into a single day.

### Bolnisi Sioni
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/bolnisi-sioni/
Region: Kvemo Kartli | type: monastery | coordinates: 41.4386, 44.5525 | elevation: 530 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 70 km / 1:25 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Bolnisi Sioni was built between 478 and 493 and is the oldest surviving church still in use in Georgia. It is a three-nave basilica, the architectural type that preceded the domed churches Georgia later became known for: relatively low, long and heavy, put together from blue-grey and yellowish tuff. That plainness is the main impression it leaves — a building that has stood for fifteen centuries in essentially unaltered form.

Its exceptional significance lies in the inscriptions. Texts in the Asomtavruli script survive on the walls, dated to around 494, placing them among the earliest dated examples of Georgian writing anywhere. For the history of the language they carry as much weight as the building does for architecture. The church also gives its name to the Bolnisi cross, the flared cross form that later entered Georgian state symbolism and appears on the national flag today.

Inside, the space is austere and almost undecorated: a row of columns, narrow windows and clean stone surfaces. The capitals carry carved reliefs of bulls, crosses and plant ornament, unusual survivals from the early Christian period and worth a close look. The church remains active with a working parish, so there are usually a few people quietly present.
Tip: This is a working church, so dress modestly: a skirt and head covering for women, long trousers for men, with wraps available at the door. An hour is enough overall, though it is worth spending some of it looking closely at the inscriptions and the carved capitals rather than only the general view. Parking in front of the yard is free. Cafés, shops and ATMs are in central Bolnisi, a few kilometres away.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi take the Marneuli highway, then turn west towards Bolnisi — about 70 km and an hour twenty-five in total. The whole route is asphalt and in good condition, so an economy car is entirely adequate. Note that the church is not in Bolnisi town itself but in a neighbouring village a few kilometres further on, so set your navigation to "Bolnisi Sioni" rather than to the town centre. Fuel is easy to find in Marneuli and Bolnisi.

### Algeti National Park
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/algeti-national-park/
Region: Kvemo Kartli | type: nature | coordinates: 41.635, 44.355 | elevation: 1200 m | time needed: 4 h | from Tbilisi: 60 km / 1:20 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: may-october | entry: free
Algeti National Park sits on the eastern slope of the Trialeti range near Manglisi and is the closest substantial forest massif to Tbilisi. Its value is primarily botanical: Oriental spruce and Caucasian fir reach the eastern limit of their range here. Further west, in the humid forests of Colchis, both species are ordinary; at Algeti they are already rare, which is precisely why the area was protected in the first place.

The park covers roughly six thousand hectares and spans altitudes from about a thousand to two thousand metres. Several marked trails have been laid out: a short ninety-minute loop from the visitor centre, and longer circuits of six to eight kilometres that climb to the ridge and open views down the Algeti valley. There are picnic areas with tables and designated tent pitches for anyone wanting to stay overnight.

Algeti is the kind of place where you can walk for hours at a weekend and meet almost nobody — organised tourism barely touches it, and Tbilisi day-trippers tend to stop at Kojori or Manglisi instead. Roe deer, wild boar and fox are present, and bears live here too, though sightings are rare. Late spring and autumn are the best seasons, with the forest at its most colourful.
Tip: Entry is free, but call at the visitor centre for a map and current trail conditions, since waymarking is damaged in places. Four hours is enough for a good day walk. Bring water and food — there is no café in the park and the nearest shop is in Manglisi. Ticks are present in the forest, so wear covered clothing and check yourself afterwards. Camping is permitted only at the designated pitches.
Route from Tbilisi: Leave Tbilisi on the Kojori road and continue towards Manglisi — about 60 km and an hour and twenty. From Kojori to Manglisi the asphalt is good but narrow and winding, with a fair amount of climbing. The last few kilometres to the park visitor centre are gravel and turn muddy after rain, so a crossover with decent ground clearance is preferable to a low economy car. Fuel and shops are available in Kojori and Manglisi, and nothing beyond them.

### Dashbashi Canyon
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/dashbashi-canyon/
Region: Kvemo Kartli | type: canyon | coordinates: 41.588, 44.048 | elevation: 1300 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 100 km / 1:50 | road: paved | car: economy | season: may-october | entry: ~50 ₾
Dashbashi Canyon lies a few kilometres from Tsalka on the edge of the Javakheti volcanic plateau. The Khrami river has cut a deep, narrow gorge through layers of basalt, and dozens of small waterfalls and springs pour straight out of the rock walls — some emerging from fissures rather than from any visible stream above. The gorge is over two hundred metres deep, and the microclimate changes as you descend: windy and dry on the plateau, humid and green down by the water.

Since 2022 the canyon's headline attraction has been the glass bridge, a structure roughly 240 metres long spanning the two rims with a diamond-shaped glass capsule suspended at its midpoint. Walking it is a commercial attraction and not cheap, and ticket prices change from time to time. Anyone uneasy with heights can skip it entirely and still get the view from the rim paths.

Beyond the bridge, trails run down into the gorge alongside the waterfalls. The descent and climb back take up to two hours in total and are steep in places. There are cafés and a large car park at the entrance complex. In winter the falls freeze into something spectacular, but the paths become slippery and are often closed after snowfall.
Tip: The glass bridge ticket is expensive and the price changes periodically, so check before you set out; walking the rim and gorge paths costs far less and many visitors find it more rewarding. Come in the morning — midday at weekends means queues on the bridge. At 1,300 metres it stays cool even in summer, so bring a jacket. Proper footwear matters: the descent into the gorge is steep and slippery when wet.
Route from Tbilisi: Take the Marneuli highway out of Tbilisi, then turn west towards Tetritskaro and Tsalka — about 100 km and an hour fifty in total. The road has been completely rebuilt in recent years and the asphalt is good, so an economy car is entirely sufficient; the only nuisance is strong crosswind on the climb up to the plateau. Fuel is available in Marneuli, Tetritskaro and Tsalka. In winter snow and ice on the plateau are common, and winter tyres are essential.

### Jvari Monastery
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/jvari-monastery/
Region: Mtskheta-Mtianeti | type: monastery | coordinates: 41.8383, 44.7325 | elevation: 650 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 27 km / 0:35 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Jvari is the building Georgian architecture starts from. It was raised between 586 and 605 on the rocky hill above Mtskheta, on the spot where Saint Nino is said to have set up the first wooden cross in the 4th century. It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1994 as part of the Historical Monuments of Mtskheta.

Architecturally it is a turning point. Jvari established the tetraconch plan — four apses around a central domed space, fully symmetrical — and that model was copied across the Caucasus for the next several centuries. The building itself is almost aggressively plain: no frescoes, no gilding, only stone, proportion and a column of light falling from the dome.

The other half of Jvari is the view. From the edge of the rock you look down on:

- The confluence of the Aragvi and the Mtkvari, where two differently coloured rivers meet without mixing at first
- Mtskheta laid out like a model, with the dome of Svetitskhoveli at its centre
- The old royal plain and the first ridges of the Greater Caucasus behind it

Lermontov wrote *Mtsyri* from this landscape, which makes the hilltop a minor pilgrimage for Russian readers as well as Orthodox ones. The monastery is active, and at night it is floodlit and visible from the town below.
Tip: Come early in the morning or towards evening; at midday coach parties arrive in waves and there is no shade at all on the rock. The wind here is strong in every season, and in winter the icy forecourt is genuinely slippery. The dress code is enforced: headscarf and long skirt for women, long trousers for men, with free wraps available at the entrance. An hour is enough. There are toilets by the car park but no café; souvenir stalls open in summer.
Route from Tbilisi: Leave Tbilisi northwards on the Georgian Military Highway (E117) and do not turn off into Mtskheta itself — the Jvari access road is a separate turning on the left bank of the river, just after the bridge. From there a narrow but fully asphalted switchback climbs about seven kilometres to the top of the cliff. The whole trip takes a little over half an hour. There is a large free car park at the summit and fuel stations at the Mtskheta turn-off. An economy car is perfectly adequate; in winter the only issue is ice on the bends.

### Svetitskhoveli Cathedral
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/svetitskhoveli-cathedral/
Region: Mtskheta-Mtianeti | type: monastery | coordinates: 41.8425, 44.7211 | elevation: 470 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 25 km / 0:30 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Svetitskhoveli is the spiritual centre of Georgia. Mtskheta was the country's capital when Christianity arrived in the 4th century, and tradition holds that the robe of Christ, brought here from Jerusalem by a Jewish Mtskhetan named Elias, is buried beneath this floor. The name means "the living pillar", after the miraculous column that is said to have raised itself during the building of the first wooden church.

The present building was completed between 1010 and 1029 by the architect Arsukisdze. It is one of the largest historical structures in Georgia, and its proportions read more powerfully inside than out. Walls, towers and a gate surround it: this was a cathedral and a fortress at the same time.

Inside you will find:

- Frescoes from the 11th to the 17th century, including a large Last Judgement on the west wall
- Royal tombs of the Bagrationi dynasty set into the floor and marked with slabs
- The presumed site of the robe, marked by a stone ciborium near the centre
- A carved right hand on the north facade, tied to the legend that the king had the architect's hand cut off so he could never build its equal

Svetitskhoveli is an active cathedral, and on Sundays it fills with baptisms and weddings. That does not block visiting; it gives the place its living context.
Tip: The dress code is enforced: headscarf and long skirt for women, long trousers for men, both handed out free at the gate. Photography inside is normally allowed without flash, though not during services. Come in the morning before the coaches or after five in the afternoon. Mtskheta is small, and cafés, toilets and ATMs are all within a couple of minutes of the cathedral walls. Allow two hours if you also walk through the old town.
Route from Tbilisi: Mtskheta lies 25 km north of Tbilisi on the Georgian Military Highway (E117), motorway the entire way and about half an hour in normal traffic. The turn-off is clearly signed; once in town the cathedral is central and its walls are visible from a distance. Traffic inside the historic core is restricted, so leave the car in the paid lot outside the walls or on the riverside parking and walk five minutes. Everything is asphalt and any car category is fine. Fuel and shops line the approach road.

### Ananuri Fortress
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/ananuri-fortress/
Region: Mtskheta-Mtianeti | type: fortress | coordinates: 42.1642, 44.7031 | elevation: 830 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 70 km / 1:20 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Ananuri is where everyone stops on the way to Kazbegi, and deservedly so. The fortress stands on a rocky spur above the Zhinvali reservoir, its lower walls dropping straight into turquoise water, and the whole composition looks almost staged.

The site developed from the 13th century onwards, but what stands today is largely 17th century. It was the seat of the Dukes of Aragvi and a defensive knot controlling the Aragvi valley — in other words, the only road north. In 1739 the rival Duke of Ksani besieged and burned it; scorch marks are still visible on the tower walls.

Three main structures sit inside the curtain wall:

- The Church of the Assumption (1689), with lavish stone carving on its south facade, a vine cross and two lions
- The older, plainer Church of the Virgin, with fragments of fresco surviving inside
- The square keep, climbable by internal stairs, with a full view over the reservoir from the top

The carving on the Assumption facade deserves a slow look; it is among the best examples of late medieval Georgian decoration anywhere. Water levels change through the year: in spring the reservoir laps close to the walls, while by late summer it drops and leaves a wide band of exposed shoreline.
Tip: An hour covers the site comfortably. The climb up the keep is a narrow, steep stone stair with no handrail, so take care in wet weather or with children. Dress rules apply inside the churches, and scarves are left by the door. Parking beside the road is free, and there are stalls selling churchkhela, honey and coffee, plus toilets. In winter the wind is fierce and the walls ice over, so proper boots make a difference.
Route from Tbilisi: Head north from Tbilisi on the Georgian Military Highway (E117) past Mtskheta and on towards Zhinvali — 70 km, about an hour and twenty minutes. The road is asphalt throughout and in good condition, though beyond Zhinvali it narrows and is cut into the cliff, so overtake with care. The fortress is directly on the right-hand side with a clear sign and a large car park. Fuel is available at Natakhtari and Zhinvali. An economy car is entirely sufficient all year round.

### Zhinvali Reservoir
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/zhinvali-reservoir/
Region: Mtskheta-Mtianeti | type: lake | coordinates: 42.14, 44.72 | elevation: 810 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 65 km / 1:15 | road: paved | car: economy | season: may-october | entry: free
Zhinvali is the point where the drive changes character. An hour out of Tbilisi the lowland scenery ends and a long, narrow, startlingly turquoise lake appears on the right, winding between wooded ridges. The colour is genuine, caused by fine mineral particles the Aragvi carries down from the mountains, and it is strongest under direct sun.

The reservoir was created in 1985 when the Zhinvali dam was completed. It supplies a large part of Tbilisi's drinking water and generates power at the same time. Old villages and medieval structures were flooded when the valley filled; in dry years, when the level drops sharply, fragments of walls reappear, which keeps local legends in good supply.

In practice Zhinvali is a stop rather than a destination:

- Roadside viewpoints between the dam and Ananuri, at almost every bend
- Ananuri fortress standing directly on the shore, so both fit into one visit
- Seasonal boat and pedalo hire in the northern arm of the lake
- Roadside cafés and trout restaurants south of the dam

The water level changes a lot through the year. In spring the reservoir is full and the colour is at its most intense; by late summer the shoreline is exposed and the effect is noticeably weaker.
Tip: Morning light or bright midday sun give the best photographs — under cloud the turquoise disappears almost completely and the water turns grey. Stop only in the marked lay-bys, because the road is narrow and standing on a bend is dangerous. Swimming near the dam is prohibited and the currents are unpredictable. Toilets and coffee are available at Ananuri and in Zhinvali village. Half an hour is plenty for the viewpoints if you are heading further north.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi head north on the Georgian Military Highway (E117) through Mtskheta and Natakhtari to Zhinvali — about 65 km and an hour and ten to fifteen minutes. After the dam the road follows the shoreline, and the next ten kilometres are the stretch with the views. The asphalt is good but narrow, cut into the rock, with plenty of blind corners, so overtake lorries carefully. Fill up in Natakhtari, as stations become scarce higher up. An economy car is entirely sufficient.

### Gudauri and the Russia–Georgia Friendship Monument
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/gudauri/
Region: Mtskheta-Mtianeti | type: ski | coordinates: 42.4783, 44.48 | elevation: 2200 m | time needed: 6 h | from Tbilisi: 120 km / 2:10 | road: paved | car: suv | season: december-march | entry: სკი-პასი ~80 ₾ დღეში
Gudauri is Georgia's largest and highest ski resort. It spreads between roughly 2,000 and 3,300 metres on the southern slope below the Jvari Pass, with more than 70 kilometres of marked pistes. The season usually runs from December to April, and the snow — dry and light — is among the best in the Caucasus.

The resort is particularly known for off-piste skiing. Heli-skiing and freeride have been established here for years, which is what distinguishes Gudauri from the gentler, more family-oriented Bakuriani. In summer the same slopes carry paragliders and mountain bikers instead.

Six kilometres above the resort, close to the pass, stands the Russia–Georgia Friendship Monument: a semicircular concrete terrace built in 1983 and lined inside with a huge colour mosaic showing scenes from the shared history of the two countries. Its political framing has aged badly, but as an object and a viewpoint it is unique — the terrace hangs over a sheer drop into the Devdoraki gorge, and the scale of the panorama is hard to convey in photographs.

Tandem paragliding flights launch from beside the monument, and in summer this is one of the most popular things visitors do in Gudauri.
Tip: Mountain weather changes several times a day here: sunshine below, cloud above, visibility down to nothing within minutes. Ski passes and rental gear are available at the resort, but queues are long over holidays. At the monument there is minimal shade and almost no railing, so hold on to children near the edge. Bring warm layers even in summer — at 2,400 metres evenings sit around ten degrees. Fuel, ATMs and cafés are in central Gudauri.
Route from Tbilisi: Take the Georgian Military Highway (E117): Tbilisi, Mtskheta, Zhinvali, Ananuri, Pasanauri, Gudauri — 120 km and about two hours ten minutes. The road is asphalt the whole way, but above Pasanauri it becomes a long climb of switchbacks shared with heavy freight traffic. In winter this section is avalanche-prone and closes periodically, so check its status before setting out. Winter tyres are mandatory in the cold season and chains are worth carrying; a crossover with decent ground clearance is far more comfortable here than a low sedan. Fill up in Pasanauri.

### Gergeti Trinity Church
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/gergeti-trinity-church/
Region: Mtskheta-Mtianeti | type: monastery | coordinates: 42.6625, 44.6206 | elevation: 2170 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 160 km / 3:10 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: may-october | entry: free
Gergeti Trinity is the image Georgia is known by. The church stands on an isolated summit above Stepantsminda at 2,170 metres, with the 5,054-metre cone of Mount Kazbek rising behind it. When the cloud clears and the glacier appears, the view really does look the way it does in photographs, which is not always true of famous places.

The church was built in the 14th century and has a separate bell tower, both in undecorated mountain stone. Its position was strategic rather than scenic: in times of invasion, relics from Mtskheta and Tbilisi were carried up here, because an attacking force could not realistically reach the summit.

There are two ways up:

- On foot from Stepantsminda through Gergeti village — one and a half to two hours of steady climbing, roughly 500 metres of ascent
- By car on the narrow concrete road, resurfaced in recent years — steep, effectively single lane, with tight hairpins and few passing places

Behind the church, trails continue towards the Gergeti glacier and the Sabertse ridge. Those are full mountain hikes and need a separate day, plus proper footwear. The church is active, monks live here, and services are held regularly, so it is not simply a viewpoint.
Tip: Kazbek is often hidden in cloud; your best chance is between seven and ten in the morning, after which cloud usually builds. Dress rules apply — headscarf and long skirt for women, long trousers for men, with wraps by the door. The wind at the top is constant and the temperature is five to seven degrees lower than in the village, so a jacket is necessary even in July. Facilities are minimal and there is no café, so buy water and food below. The nearest ATM is in central Stepantsminda.
Route from Tbilisi: Head north from Tbilisi on the Georgian Military Highway through Zhinvali, Ananuri, Pasanauri and Gudauri, over the Jvari Pass at 2,379 metres, then down through Kobi to Stepantsminda — 155 km and about three hours. From the village it is a further 6 km up a steep, narrow concrete road. A sedan can technically manage it in dry conditions, but a crossover or 4x4 is what you actually want, since passing an oncoming car means putting two wheels on dirt. In winter chains and four-wheel drive are essential. Fuel in Pasanauri or Stepantsminda.

### Dariali Gorge and the Gveleti Waterfalls
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/dariali-gorge-gveleti-waterfalls/
Region: Mtskheta-Mtianeti | type: waterfall | coordinates: 42.7205, 44.627 | elevation: 1550 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 170 km / 3:25 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: may-october | entry: პარკირება ~5 ₾
Dariali is where the mountains almost close the road. North of Stepantsminda the Terek valley suddenly narrows and squeezes between granite walls three hundred metres high. This is historically the main gateway through the Caucasus, called the Caspian or Caucasian Gates by ancient authors. The gorge runs up to the Russian border, and this is the last point on the route that a rental car can legally reach.

Halfway along, above Gveleti village, are two waterfalls:

- The lower Gveleti falls, about fifteen minutes from the road and manageable for almost anyone
- The upper Gveleti falls, roughly 25 metres high, another twenty to thirty minutes further up over boulders

The trail is short but not flat: loose blocks, tree roots and wet rock in the shaded sections. May and June are the best months, when snowmelt gives the falls their maximum volume; by late August the upper cascade thins noticeably.

Also in the gorge stands the Dariali Monastery, a modern complex built in the 2000s. It is new, but it sits surprisingly well against the cliffs and makes a natural last stop before the frontier zone begins.
Tip: Wear proper closed shoes with grip — sandals are useless on this trail. Near the falls the air is cold and the spray soaks clothing, so bring a windproof layer. This is a border zone: carry your passport or ID, as the border police do check. There is a small paid car park at the trailhead, usually with a kiosk. Buy food and water in Stepantsminda, because there is nothing at all further up the valley.
Route from Tbilisi: From Stepantsminda follow the main road north along the Terek — 12 to 15 km, about twenty minutes. From Tbilisi it is 170 km in total and roughly three and a half hours. The main road is asphalt, though rockfall debris on the surface is routine here. The Gveleti turning is on the left after the bridge, and the last couple of kilometres are gravel, which is precisely why a crossover is preferable to a sedan. Do not drive up to the border crossing itself: taking a rental car out of Georgia is not permitted.

### Truso Valley
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/truso-valley/
Region: Mtskheta-Mtianeti | type: mountain | coordinates: 42.535, 44.395 | elevation: 2100 m | time needed: 6 h | from Tbilisi: 145 km / 3:00 | road: gravel | car: offroad | season: june-september | entry: free
Truso is the valley where there is almost nobody. It begins near Kobi, south of Kazbegi, and runs west for more than fifteen kilometres towards the headwaters of the Terek, through bare, treeless, almost Central Asian scenery. It is a border zone, and that restriction is largely why it has stayed unchanged.

The defining feature is mineral water. Carbon-dioxide-rich springs rise through the valley floor, depositing calcium carbonate as they cool, and over centuries these have built travertine terraces — orange, yellow and white cascades that from a distance look like frozen waterfalls. The best known are the Abano springs.

Along the track you pass:

- Abano lake, a small pool of vividly coloured mineral water
- Abandoned villages with stone defensive towers: Ketrisi, Abano and Resi
- Zakagori fortress on a rock spur towards the far end of the valley
- Alpine pasture with sheep flocks and temporary shepherds' camps

Truso is not a one-hour stop; it is a full day. Many travellers leave the car at the mouth of the valley and walk ten to twelve kilometres in and back, which is arguably the best way to do it if you have the time and the weather is settled.
Tip: This is a border zone: carry a passport or ID, because there is a border police post at the entrance and they do check. The season runs from June to September, and the rest of the year the track is closed by snow. There is no shade anywhere and the sun at 2,200 metres is harsh, so bring a hat, sunscreen and at least two litres of water per person. No shops, no toilets and effectively no mobile signal — stock up in Kobi or Stepantsminda.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi take the Military Highway over the Jvari Pass and turn off at Kobi — 145 km, around three hours. From Kobi into Truso the road is gravel: fifteen kilometres of stony, rutted track with several river fords. A sedan is not an option here; you need real ground clearance and preferably four-wheel drive. After heavy rain the fords rise and the track can become impassable altogether. Fill up in Pasanauri or Gudauri, as there is no fuel in the valley. Choose the vehicle in advance from the fleet.

### Shatili
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/shatili/
Region: Mtskheta-Mtianeti | type: fortress | coordinates: 42.6572, 45.1608 | elevation: 1400 m | time needed: 4 h | from Tbilisi: 155 km / 4:30 | road: 4x4_only | car: offroad | season: june-september | entry: ~5 ₾
Shatili is not a collection of houses but a single grown organism. On the northern edge of Khevsureti, in the Arghuni gorge, some fifty stone towers and dwellings are built into and onto each other on a steep slope. They rise in terraces, one roof serving as another's yard, and together they form an indivisible defensive system: in the Middle Ages the entire village was one fortress.

Most of the structures date from the 9th to the 13th century. For centuries the Khevsurs held this frontier against raids from the north, and Shatili was its last outpost. In the 1950s the population was forcibly resettled to the lowlands; today the village is partly inhabited again and several towers have been converted into guesthouses.

Around Shatili:

- The Anatori crypts, 3 km away, stone tombs where plague victims are said to have walked in to die rather than infect the village
- Mutso, another fortress-village 12 km further on, wilder and almost entirely abandoned
- The Arghuni gorge itself, narrow, deep and within the border zone

This is one of the remotest places in Georgia that you can still drive to, and staying overnight is close to obligatory: doing it as a day trip from Tbilisi is punishing.
Tip: The season is short — mid-June to late September, since the Datvijvari Pass at 2,676 m is snowbound the rest of the year. Book accommodation ahead: Shatili has only a handful of guesthouses and they fill in August. There is essentially no mobile signal and no ATM, so bring cash. It is a border zone, so a passport is required. Pack warm clothing even in August, when nights drop to five or eight degrees.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi take the Military Highway to Zhinvali, then turn right towards Barisakho up the Aragvi valley. Asphalt continues to Barisakho; after that comes roughly 60 km of gravel over the Datvijvari Pass — narrow, unbarriered, with steep descents and loose rock. In total 155 km and at least four and a half hours, more after rain. Only a proper 4x4 with good tyres belongs on this road; an ordinary crossover is a gamble. Take your last fuel at Zhinvali or Barisakho, as there is no station in Shatili.

### Nikortsminda Cathedral
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/nikortsminda-cathedral/
Region: Racha-Lechkhumi | type: monastery | coordinates: 42.4467, 43.0264 | elevation: 1050 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 300 km / 5:10 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Nikortsminda stands in a small village about thirteen kilometres before Ambrolauri and is regarded as the principal historic monument of Racha. The cathedral was built between 1010 and 1014 under Bagrat III, in the same wave of construction that produced the great churches of the newly united kingdom.

What sets Nikortsminda apart is the stone carving on its facades. Cornices, window frames and the drum of the dome are covered in relief work: geometric ornament, vine scrolls, animal and human figures, apostles. In terms of sheer density of decoration it is among the richest examples in medieval Georgian architecture, and it deserves time spent looking closely rather than a glance from the gate.

Inside are wall paintings of the 16th and 17th centuries, remarkably well preserved. The bell tower is a later addition from the 19th century.

Worth looking for:

- the reliefs on the north and west facades
- the carved drum of the dome and the window surrounds
- the interior frescoes in the sanctuary and under the dome

The cathedral is active and open almost all the time. It sits on Georgia's UNESCO tentative list, but is not inscribed on the World Heritage List. A visit takes about fifty minutes and makes the natural first stop on entering Racha.
Tip: This is a working church: women need a headscarf and long skirt, men long trousers. Midday is the worst time for the carving — low side light in the morning or late afternoon brings out the relief far better. The interior is dark and your eyes need a few minutes to adjust before the frescoes read properly. Park in front of the yard. Toilets are basic; the nearest cafe and ATM are in Ambrolauri, thirteen kilometres on.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi take the E60 towards Kutaisi, then turn north through Tkibuli and climb the mountain road into Racha; Nikortsminda sits right by the road shortly before Ambrolauri. Around 300 km and five hours in total. Asphalt runs the whole way, but the last sixty kilometres are narrow, cut into rock and full of bends where passing an oncoming car takes attention. In winter this section ices over. Fill up in Kutaisi or Tkibuli, as options thin out beyond.

### Shaori Reservoir
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/shaori-reservoir/
Region: Racha-Lechkhumi | type: lake | coordinates: 42.475, 43.1 | elevation: 1130 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 305 km / 5:15 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: may-october | entry: free
Shaori lies on the Racha plateau at roughly 1,130 metres above sea level. It is not a natural lake: the reservoir was created in the Soviet period to feed a hydroelectric scheme, flooding the Shaori basin. Traces of that remain visible — when the water level drops, the stumps of old trees and the outlines of drowned fields appear along the shore.

Pine forest and meadow surround the water, with the ridges of Racha standing on the horizon. This is one of the few places in the region with genuinely wide open space; the rest of Racha is narrow gorges and dense forest.

What people do here:

- camp along the shore, especially in July and August
- fish, mainly for carp and trout
- walk the shoreline and the pine woods
- stop for a picnic on the way out from Nikortsminda or Ambrolauri

Swimming is possible, though the water is high-altitude cold and stays cool even in July.

In winter the lake partly freezes and the access road fills with snow, so between November and April the trip is not worth making. The best window is June to September, when the meadows are green and evening temperatures are comfortable.
Tip: There is essentially no infrastructure: no cafe, no toilets, no shop at the shore. Bring water, food and a rubbish bag, and carry your waste back out. If you camp, pitch on dry ground sheltered from the wind — nights drop towards ten degrees even in August. Insect repellent is not optional here in midsummer. The nearest fuel and ATM are in Ambrolauri, about thirty kilometres away.
Route from Tbilisi: The approach is the same as for Nikortsminda: E60 towards Kutaisi, then north through Tkibuli and up the mountain road into Racha. Past Nikortsminda turn east and drive about twenty kilometres to the lake — around 305 km and five hours fifteen in total. The last stretch is partly gravel and turns muddy after rain, which is where extra ground clearance genuinely helps. In winter the road is closed by snow, and there is no maintained alternative.

### Shovi Resort
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/shovi-resort/
Region: Racha-Lechkhumi | type: mountain | coordinates: 42.6819, 43.6822 | elevation: 1520 m | time needed: 4 h | from Tbilisi: 395 km / 6:50 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: june-september | entry: free
Shovi sits in Oni municipality in the valley of the Chanchakhi river, at about 1,520 metres. It developed in the Soviet period as a climatic and mineral water resort: pine forest, cool air and views towards the main Caucasus ridge made it the summer destination of Racha.

In August 2023 a large debris flow swept down the valley, destroying part of the resort and causing loss of life. Recovery and slope-stabilisation work has been under way since, some of the infrastructure no longer exists, and the situation continues to change. For that reason check road conditions and whether accommodation is operating before you set out — this is not somewhere to arrive on spec.

If the road is open and the weather is dry, Shovi remains a striking place:

- the Chanchakhi gorge and the high ridges of the Caucasus
- pine forest and mineral springs
- the starting point for routes towards Glola and Ghebi

The season is short, roughly June to September. In winter the road closes with snow, and in spring the risk of flooding and debris flows is high. This valley reacts sharply to weather, and heavy rain is a good reason to be somewhere else that day.
Tip: Before setting out, call a hotel or the Oni municipality and confirm the state of the road and what is actually operating — this changes from season to season. If heavy rain is forecast, postpone the trip rather than risk the valley. Warm clothing is essential even in summer, as nights fall towards five degrees. Fill the tank in Ambrolauri or Oni, since there is no fuel higher up. Mobile coverage in the gorge is unreliable.
Route from Tbilisi: Follow the usual approach into Racha: from Tbilisi towards Kutaisi, north through Tkibuli to Ambrolauri, then east to Oni and up the Chanchakhi valley to Shovi. Around 395 km and close to seven hours one way, which makes this a full day of driving on its own. Asphalt is mostly decent as far as Oni; above that there are gravel sections and stretches repaired since the disaster. Real ground clearance is advisable. Plan an overnight stop in Ambrolauri or Oni rather than attempting a return run.

### Udziro Lake and Buba Glacier (Ghebi)
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/udziro-lake-buba-glacier/
Region: Racha-Lechkhumi | type: mountain | coordinates: 42.7086, 43.7156 | elevation: 1300 m | time needed: 8 h | from Tbilisi: 410 km / 7:20 | road: 4x4_only | car: offroad | season: june-september | entry: free
Ghebi is the final village in Racha: the road ends here and beyond it there are only trails climbing towards the main Caucasus ridge. Two routes matter from the village — Udziro Lake, a high mountain lake lying above 2,500 metres, and the Buba glacier valley, from which the Buba and Chiukhi peaks come into view.

It is important to understand what reaching them involves: the car only gets you as far as Ghebi. From there both the lake and the glacier are reached on foot — a full day, several hours in each direction, requiring decent fitness and, on some sections, fording a river. Many groups camp overnight rather than attempt a return in one push.

What to weigh up:

- the season is very short, realistically July to mid-September
- snowfields remain high up even in June, and the path is not always obvious
- weather changes several times a day and cloud drops fast
- mobile coverage effectively ends above the village
- a local guide here is a sensible decision rather than a luxury

This route is for experienced travellers. If it is your first time in the Georgian mountains, driving as far as Ghebi and seeing the valley is worthwhile on its own, without attempting the climb to the lake.
Tip: This is not a day outing: reaching the lake or the glacier takes a full day and often an overnight camp. Bring hiking boots, a rain shell, a warm layer, food, and either a water filter or your own supply. Arrange a guide in Ghebi before walking up, because the trail is not waymarked throughout. Shops and fuel are back in Oni and there is nothing above. Check the weather forecast before you commit to the drive.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi head towards Kutaisi, north through Tkibuli to Ambrolauri, then east to Oni and on through Glola to Ghebi — roughly 410 km and over seven hours. Beyond Oni the asphalt ends and the road becomes gravel, stony and washed out in places, with several stream crossings. This section requires a genuine high-clearance 4x4; a sedan or an ordinary crossover has no business attempting it. Plan an overnight in Oni or Ghebi rather than driving back the same day.

### Tsageri and Lechkhumi
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/tsageri/
Region: Racha-Lechkhumi | type: town | coordinates: 42.6444, 42.7669 | elevation: 480 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 325 km / 5:00 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: may-october | entry: free
Tsageri is the administrative centre of Lechkhumi, set in the valley of the Tskhenistskali river at around 480 metres. It is a small, quiet town with minimal tourist infrastructure, and that is precisely its appeal. Compared with the high mountain routes of Racha, Lechkhumi is far more accessible and stays open through the whole season.

Lechkhumi is above all wine country. Rare varieties are grown here, including Usakhelouri, produced in tiny quantities and regarded as one of the most expensive red wines in Georgia. Family cellars in Tsageri and the surrounding villages offer tastings, usually by prior arrangement.

A day here typically covers:

- the centre of Tsageri, its market and old church
- Muri fortress above the valley
- the Lajanuri reservoir, with its turquoise water
- family wine cellars in the valley villages

Tsageri also works as a staging point on the way towards Svaneti, though that leg needs planning of its own. If you are already heading into Racha, Lechkhumi is a natural addition that costs little extra driving and gives the trip a lower-altitude, gentler second half.
Tip: Arrange cellar tastings in advance — Lechkhumi producers are small operations and Usakhelouri is not always available. Decide who is driving before the tasting begins, since Georgia enforces a strict alcohol limit. Carry cash, as cards are not accepted everywhere. There is fuel in Tsageri but little choice of station, and an ATM in the centre. Guesthouses are modest, and booking ahead in season is sensible.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi take the E60 to Kutaisi, then head north into the valley towards Tsageri — around 325 km and five hours in total. Past Kutaisi the road narrows and follows the Tskhenistskali gorge: asphalt exists for most of it but is broken in places, and several village turnoffs are gravel. Extra ground clearance improves the drive considerably. In winter the road remains passable but ices over. Fill the tank in Kutaisi, where the choice is far better.

### Mestia and the Svan Towers
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/mestia/
Region: Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti | type: town | coordinates: 43.045, 42.728 | elevation: 1500 m | time needed: 4 h | from Tbilisi: 470 km / 8:30 | road: paved | car: suv | season: may-october | entry: free
Mestia is the administrative and tourist centre of Upper Svaneti, sitting at roughly 1,500 metres in the upper Enguri gorge. What makes it unusual is that its history is not locked inside a museum: the stone defence towers, most of them dating from the ninth to thirteenth centuries, still stand in ordinary family yards. Svan households built them for two overlapping reasons — protection from raiders, and shelter during avalanches and the long blood-feud disputes that shaped local law.

The old quarters of Lanchvali, Lagami and Lekhtagi are separated by footbridges and narrow lanes, and you can walk the lot in half a day. The Svaneti Museum of History and Ethnography holds processional crosses, icons, chased metalwork and manuscripts that survived precisely because the region was so hard to reach; several pieces were hidden in mountain churches for centuries. The Mikheil Khergiani House-Museum, in the tower house of Georgia's most famous climber, is worth a separate half hour.

What you will actually see:

- Machubi — the traditional Svan house where family and livestock wintered in one hall
- Seti Square — the town centre, with cafes, the information point and the guide exchange
- The Cross viewpoint — a short climb above town with the twin summits of Ushba ahead

Mestia is also a base. Routes to the Chalaadi glacier, the Koruldi lakes, the Hatsvali and Tetnuldi ski areas and Ushguli all start here, and the choice of guesthouses and food is the widest in the region.
Tip: Plan at least two nights in Mestia; a single-day visit is mostly driving. Late June to late September is the reliable window. The town works in winter too, but the road occasionally closes after avalanches. Weather changes several times a day, so a rain shell and a warm layer are needed even in August. Park at your guesthouse or on the streets around Seti Square and walk everywhere — the centre is tiny. ATMs and a pharmacy are in the centre, but card payment is not universal, so carry some cash in lari.
Route from Tbilisi: Mestia is about 470 km and eight to nine hours from Tbilisi. Take the E60 west through Kutaisi and Samtredia to Zugdidi, then turn north past the Enguri dam at Jvari and into the gorge. The 130 km from Zugdidi to Mestia is fully paved but narrow and endlessly winding — count on three hours for that stretch alone. Doing it in one day is possible, but an overnight stop in Kutaisi or Zugdidi makes the trip far more pleasant. The last dependable fuel stations are in Zugdidi and Jvari. A crossover is more comfortable on the long switchbacks, though a sedan will manage.

### Ushguli
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/ushguli/
Region: Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti | type: town | coordinates: 42.9155, 43.0136 | elevation: 2100 m | time needed: 4 h | from Tbilisi: 515 km / 10:30 | road: gravel | car: offroad | season: june-september | entry: ~5 ₾
Ushguli is the collective name for four closely spaced villages — Chazhashi, Chvibiani, Zhibiani and Murqmeli — standing at the head of the Enguri valley at roughly 2,100 metres. It is regularly described as one of the highest permanently inhabited places in Europe. Since 1996 it has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list as part of the Upper Svaneti site; what is protected is not a single monument but the whole historic pattern of settlement, with its towers, houses and hay meadows.

The view is the main event. Shkhara, Georgia's highest summit at 5,193 metres, rises directly behind the villages and closes the valley. On a low hill above Zhibiani stands Lamaria church, a small twelfth-century building with surviving frescoes and its own defensive tower. In Chazhashi an ethnographic museum displays icons, weapons and household objects.

Things worth knowing in advance:

- In winter the village is often cut off — snow can close the road for weeks at a time
- The final stretch from Mestia is unpaved and genuinely needs a high-clearance vehicle
- Services are minimal — a handful of guesthouses, small cafes, no ATM

Ushguli is not a packaged attraction, and that is exactly its value. It remains a working village: people still keep cattle and cut hay on the same slopes their families worked more than a century ago, while visitors walk between the towers.
Tip: Leave Mestia in the morning, before 09:00 — it is two hours each way and you do not want to drive the gravel back in the dark. Walking the four villages takes two to three hours, plus about forty minutes for the climb to Lamaria church. Dress modestly inside the church: a headscarf and a long skirt for women. Park at the marked area by the village entrance and continue on foot, since the lanes are narrow and livestock wanders freely. Bring cash; toilets are in the cafes.
Route from Tbilisi: Ushguli is roughly 515 km from Tbilisi, which realistically means a two-day approach with a night in Mestia. From Mestia it is 45–47 km and about two hours: asphalt at first, then a gravel and stone road that crosses the river several times and deteriorates sharply after rain. That is precisely why a high-clearance vehicle is required here — a low car is neither safe nor covered by rental insurance on this section. The last fuel is in Mestia, so fill the tank before you set off, and check the weather, as heavy rain can make the fords slow.

### Chalaadi Glacier
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/chalaadi-glacier/
Region: Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti | type: mountain | coordinates: 43.12, 42.77 | elevation: 1900 m | time needed: 4 h | from Tbilisi: 480 km / 8:50 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: june-september | entry: free
The Chalaadi glacier flows down from the main Caucasus ridge and is the easiest glacier to reach from Mestia. That makes it the logical choice for a first full day in Svaneti: no guide, no mountaineering equipment and no dawn start are required.

The route is straightforward. From Mestia you drive north-east up the Mestiachala valley for about seven kilometres to a small parking area where the road ends. From there a path crosses the river on a suspension bridge, climbs through birch and alder forest, and then works its way up loose glacial moraine. It is roughly an hour each way, or up to three hours in total with stops and photographs.

What you will see:

- The suspension bridge over the Mestiachala — it sways, but it is entirely safe
- Dense riverside forest that gives way abruptly to bare glacial rubble
- The ice tongue itself, grey-brown with debris, with meltwater caves at its base

Keep expectations realistic. Like most glaciers in the Caucasus, Chalaadi is retreating, so the ice edge sits slightly further back each year. Climbing onto the ice or entering the caves is strongly discouraged: the surface is unstable and collapses are common. From the lower moraine the view is more than enough to grasp the scale of the thing.
Tip: Start in the morning. Cloud usually fills the valley after midday and rain follows. Wear proper walking shoes with grip — the last section crosses loose stone and is unpleasant in trainers. Carry water and a snack, since nothing is reliably sold at the trailhead. Temperatures drop sharply at the ice, so bring a jacket even in July. The walk is manageable with children if they are comfortable on the swinging bridge. Allow about three hours from car to car and do not plan anything tight afterwards.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi you first drive to Mestia — 470 km and eight to nine hours via Zugdidi and the Enguri gorge. From Mestia it is roughly seven to nine kilometres up the Mestiachala valley to the trailhead parking. The first part is asphalt; the last few kilometres are gravel with potholes and shallow drainage cuts. In dry weather a crossover handles it easily, while with a sedan it is better to stop a kilometre early and walk. Fill up in Mestia, as there is no fuel in the valley. Local drivers also run transfers from the town centre if you would rather not take your own car up.

### Koruldi Lakes
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/koruldi-lakes/
Region: Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti | type: lake | coordinates: 43.081, 42.712 | elevation: 2740 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 480 km / 9:30 | road: 4x4_only | car: offroad | season: june-september | entry: free
The Koruldi lakes are a cluster of small, sometimes almost seasonal alpine pools on the ridge above Mestia, at around 2,740 metres. The lakes themselves are modest: they are fullest in June and can shrink dramatically by late August. The point of coming here is the view. To the north the twin towers of Ushba rise to 4,710 metres, Tetnuldi closes the eastern skyline, and the whole Mestia valley with its tower houses sits in the frame below.

The ascent begins past the Cross viewpoint above town: first a steep dirt track, then a stony path across high summer pastures. On foot it takes four to five hours each way, which is why most visitors hire a local 4x4 and make it a ninety-minute drive instead.

What to expect:

- This is not a general-purpose road — it is a deeply rutted, rocky mountain track
- The season is short — snow lingers into mid-June and returns from late September
- The view depends entirely on weather — on a cloudy day Ushba simply is not there

If the sky is not clear, the trip loses most of its purpose and is worth postponing a day. On a clean morning, though, this is the most striking panorama in Svaneti, and it requires no technical skill to reach.
Tip: Check the forecast the evening before and go early: after about 11:00 cloud usually closes over Ushba. If you drive yourself, only a genuine high-clearance 4x4 will do — an ordinary crossover has no business on this track and would not be covered by insurance. The simple alternative is to take one of the local drivers who run up from Mestia centre several times a day. It is windy at the top and eight to ten degrees colder than in town, so bring a jacket and a hat. There are no facilities up there.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi you first reach Mestia — 470 km and around nine hours via Zugdidi. From Mestia the lakes are only 10–12 km away, but the entire distance is a steep dirt mountain track that passes the Cross viewpoint and climbs onto open pasture, taking about ninety minutes each way. A high-clearance 4x4 with low range is the right tool; after rain the ruts get considerably worse and the surface turns greasy. Fuel is available in Mestia and nowhere above it. If your rental category does not cover this kind of surface, hiring a local jeep is the sensible choice.

### Hatsvali and Tetnuldi Ski Areas
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/hatsvali-tetnuldi/
Region: Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti | type: ski | coordinates: 43.0083, 42.7364 | elevation: 1870 m | time needed: 6 h | from Tbilisi: 478 km / 8:50 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: december-march | entry: ~30 ₾
Upper Svaneti has two ski areas, and they complement each other rather than compete. Hatsvali lies eight kilometres from Mestia, starts at about 1,870 metres and is defined by runs cut through forest: short, sheltered from wind and comfortable for intermediate skiers. Its gondola also operates in summer, and plenty of visitors ride it in July and August purely for the view.

Tetnuldi sits 15–16 kilometres from Mestia, higher and considerably more serious. Its lift system takes skiers above three thousand metres, opening onto wide treeless slopes. This is one of the highest lift-served points in Georgia, and the panorama across Shkhara, Ushba and Tetnuldi itself justifies the ticket on its own.

The practical differences:

- Hatsvali — short access road, forest runs, less wind, modest vertical
- Tetnuldi — longer and partly rough access, alpine terrain, much bigger descent
- Both areas run a short season and have simpler infrastructure than Gudauri

Equipment rental exists at both bases, but the range is limited, so bring your own boots if you have them. Regular transfers run from Mestia centre to each area, which many people prefer to driving. Neither resort has the queues or the nightlife of larger Georgian resorts, and that is a large part of the appeal here.
Tip: The season runs roughly from late December to late March, though snow quality varies sharply from year to year, so check conditions before committing. Both bases have a small cafe but no ATM: carry cash in lari. Tetnuldi is colder and windier, so a face mask and warm gloves are genuinely needed. Parking at each base is free and rarely full. Winter tyres are compulsory in the season and chains are worth having in the car, particularly for the upper part of the Tetnuldi road.
Route from Tbilisi: Tbilisi to Mestia is 470 km and eight to nine hours via Zugdidi and the Enguri gorge. From Mestia, Hatsvali is eight kilometres of paved switchbacks, about twenty minutes. Tetnuldi is 15–16 km and takes over half an hour: part of the road is asphalt, part is gravel and gets churned up in winter. That is why a high-clearance car on winter tyres is the sensible choice here. Fill up in Mestia, since there is no fuel at either base. In poor weather an organised transfer from town is the easier option.

### Martvili Canyon
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/martvili-canyon/
