Region: Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti | type: canyon | coordinates: 42.4747, 42.6111 | elevation: 200 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 310 km / 4:30 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~20 ₾ + ნავი ~15 ₾
Martvili Canyon was cut by the Abasha river through limestone and runs for roughly two kilometres. Its defining feature is the colour of the water: dissolved limestone gives the river a milky turquoise tone that is most intense on a sunny day once the spring flood has passed.

Historically this was a bathing spot for the Dadiani princes of Mingrelia, and the pool they had carved into the rock is still visible. The site is now run by the Agency of Protected Areas and is properly developed: wooden walkways are fixed to the canyon walls, with footbridges and viewing platforms along the way. For an additional fee there is a short inflatable-boat ride, roughly 300 metres through the narrowest section.

What a visit involves:

- A boardwalk along the canyon with several viewpoints
- Small side waterfalls dropping in from tributary gullies, fullest in spring
- The boat trip — brief, but the only way to see the walls from water level

Most people spend an hour and a half to two hours here. Nearby are the Balda and Gachedili canyons, both considerably quieter, which combine well with Martvili into a single day. Together they make Samegrelo worth a stop rather than just a stretch of road on the way to Svaneti or the coast.
Tip: Come early or after mid-afternoon: between 11:00 and 15:00, especially on summer weekends, the queue for the boat can reach half an hour or more. Wear shoes with grip, as the boardwalk gets slippery after rain. You will get wet in the boat, so put your phone in a waterproof pouch. There is parking, a toilet and a cafe at the entrance. In early spring the river runs high and muddy and the boats sometimes do not operate at all, which is worth checking before you plan around it.
Route from Tbilisi: Martvili is about 310 km and four and a half hours from Tbilisi. Take the E60 west through Gori, Khashuri, the new Rikoti tunnel section and Kutaisi, continue toward Samtredia and then turn north to Martvili. The motorway part is good asphalt throughout, and the final 20 km is a narrow but entirely sound regional road. An economy car is perfectly adequate. Fill up in Kutaisi or Samtredia; there is fuel in Martvili town too, but the choice of stations is limited. The turn-off is signposted and easy to follow.

### Enguri Dam and Jvari Reservoir
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/enguri-dam/
Region: Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti | type: lake | coordinates: 42.7677, 42.0311 | elevation: 300 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 350 km / 5:10 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
The Enguri dam is the first genuinely large thing you meet on the road from Zugdidi up to Mestia. It stands roughly 271 metres high, which places it among the tallest arch dams in the world. Construction began in the 1960s and the structure reached its final form in the 1980s; it remains one of the most important elements of Georgia's power system.

There are two quite different things to look at. First, the structure itself — a thin curved concrete wall plugging a narrow gorge between two rock faces, with a genuinely vertiginous drop below. Second, the Jvari reservoir: a long, branching lake behind the dam whose water turns intensely turquoise in summer because of suspended limestone silt.

In practice you will see:

- The viewpoint on the dam crest — the main shot, reachable straight from the road
- The shore road toward Mestia, where the view over the water keeps changing
- Jvari settlement with small cafes and a fuel station

This is not a half-day destination; thirty to sixty minutes is normal. But as a first stop on the long drive into Svaneti it is natural and well placed, and it gives a sense of the scale of the gorge you are about to spend three hours driving through.
Tip: The best light is from morning to early afternoon, while the sun still reaches into the gorge. Stopping on the dam crest means parking in a tight spot: pull fully off the carriageway and put your hazards on, because this is a busy transit road with trucks. The dam is a strategic facility, so drone flights and some viewpoints may be restricted — read the signs on site rather than assuming. Drinking water and toilets are in Jvari settlement, not at the dam itself.
Route from Tbilisi: It is about 350 km and five hours from Tbilisi. Take the E60 west through Kutaisi and Samtredia to Zugdidi, then turn north-east toward Jvari: from Zugdidi to the dam is only 30 km, roughly forty minutes. The road is paved throughout and an economy car is entirely sufficient. Fill up in Zugdidi, the last place with a proper choice of stations before the mountains. If you are heading to Mestia the dam is directly on your route, so no detour is needed — simply build in a short stop.

### Dadiani Palace, Zugdidi
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/dadiani-palace-zugdidi/
Region: Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti | type: museum | coordinates: 42.5089, 41.8714 | elevation: 100 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 320 km / 4:40 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~15 ₾
The Dadiani Palace stands in the historic centre of Zugdidi and was the seat of the Dadiani family, hereditary princes of Mingrelia. The complex was built in the nineteenth century and includes several buildings, a palace church and an extensive botanical garden that still serves as the town's main park.

Its best-known exhibit is one of the small number of authentic death masks of Napoleon Bonaparte. It reached Georgia through marriage: Salome Dadiani married Achille Murat, grandson of Napoleon's marshal Joachim Murat, and part of the family collection came to Zugdidi with her. The palace rooms also hold Georgian chased metalwork, icons, manuscripts, furniture and the personal effects of the princely family.

What you will see:

- The main palace, with displays arranged close to the historic interiors
- The botanical garden, laid out in the nineteenth century with exotic trees
- The palace church within the grounds

Zugdidi is mostly treated as a town you pass through on the way to Svaneti, and many travellers skip it entirely. The palace is the thing that makes stopping worthwhile: it shows that lowland Mingrelia had its own princely history, quite separate from the mountain world of Svaneti an hour and a half to the north.
Tip: Allow an hour and a half to two hours including a walk in the garden. Opening arrangements change with the season and Monday is often a closing day, so check before you build a day around it. English labelling is patchy, which makes a guide or audio guide worth the extra fee. Photography is restricted in some rooms. Park on the square in front of the palace or on the adjoining street, both free. Cafes and ATMs are a two-minute walk away in the town centre.
Route from Tbilisi: Zugdidi is about 320 km and four and a half to five hours from Tbilisi. The route runs almost entirely on the E60: Gori, Khashuri, the new Rikoti section, Kutaisi, Samtredia, then north-west to Zugdidi. The road is paved and in good condition throughout, so an economy car is entirely sufficient. Fill up in Kutaisi or Samtredia; Zugdidi also has a reasonable choice of stations. The palace sits in the town centre and is signposted from the main approach, with parking directly in front of the gates.

### Nokalakevi (Archaeopolis)
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/nokalakevi/
Region: Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti | type: archaeology | coordinates: 42.3628, 42.1817 | elevation: 90 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 300 km / 4:30 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~10 ₾
Nokalakevi is one of the most important archaeological sites in western Georgia. Byzantine authors knew it as Archaeopolis, while Georgian tradition called it Tsikhegoji. It occupies a naturally defended position in the valley of the Tekhuri river and was a principal centre of the kingdom of Egrisi between the fourth and sixth centuries.

Its historical weight comes from the Lazic Wars, the sixth-century contest between Byzantium and Sasanian Persia for control of western Georgia. Nokalakevi was one of the key fortified nodes in that conflict, and the surviving walls reflect the military engineering of exactly that period.

What you will find on site:

- The lower fortress walls and towers, partly consolidated and restored
- A secret tunnel cut down through the rock to the Tekhuri, built to supply water during a siege
- The remains of a basilica and a bath house
- A small museum displaying finds from the excavations

A joint Georgian-British archaeological expedition has worked here for many years, so in summer you may well see active trenches and researchers at work. The climb to the upper fortress is steep and unshaded, but the view along the valley makes it worth the effort, and it clarifies exactly why the site was chosen.
Tip: Allow an hour and a half to two hours. Wear comfortable shoes: the ground is grassy and sloping, and the stairway down the water tunnel is narrow and damp, so a phone torch helps. Summers here are hot and humid, which makes a morning visit far more pleasant than midday, and you should carry water. Park on the small area by the entrance. The nearest cafes and ATM are in Senaki, so take cash with you before you arrive.
Route from Tbilisi: Nokalakevi is about 300 km and four and a half hours from Tbilisi. Follow the E60 west through Khashuri, the Rikoti section, Kutaisi and Samtredia, then turn toward Senaki and continue a few kilometres north to the site. The whole route is paved; the final stretch is a narrow village road but in sound condition, so an economy car is sufficient. Fill up in Samtredia or Senaki. The site combines well with Martvili Canyon in a single day, since both lie within about forty minutes of each other.

### Vardzia
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/vardzia/
Region: Samtskhe-Javakheti | type: cave | coordinates: 41.3811, 43.2847 | elevation: 1300 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 265 km / 4:20 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~15 ₾ + შატლი ~3 ₾
Vardzia is carved into a sheer tufa cliff on the left bank of the Mtkvari, stretching for the better part of a kilometre. Work began under George III and was completed in the reign of Queen Tamar. It was never only a monastery: this was a fortified frontier town, with refectories, a water supply system, wine presses, storerooms and hundreds of living cells linked into one honeycombed structure that could shelter an army.

Originally the halls sat deep inside the rock and were almost invisible from the valley floor. A powerful earthquake in the 13th century sheared away the outer face of the cliff and exposed the interior — which is exactly why the site looks the way it does today, sliced open like a cross-section drawing.

The centrepiece is the Church of the Dormition, which holds original 12th-century frescoes, including portraits of Queen Tamar and George III. Tamar is shown during her own lifetime, which makes the painting an unusually direct piece of medieval evidence.

What you actually walk through:

- terraced paths and stairways between levels, with short tunnels in places
- the frescoed main church
- the bell tower and upper galleries, with the full sweep of the gorge below

Part of the complex is still an active monastery, and a small community of monks lives on site.
Tip: Come early morning or after 16:00 — the gorge bakes at midday and tour groups arrive in the middle of the day. Leave the car at the lower parking area; a small shuttle runs up to the entrance, or you can walk it in about fifteen minutes uphill. Wear shoes with grip: the stone is polished and the stairs are steep. Bring water and a hat, since there is almost no shade. Women need a headscarf and skirt for the church. Cafe and toilets sit by the entrance; the nearest ATM is in Aspindza.
Route from Tbilisi: Take the E60 west from Tbilisi past Mtskheta and Gori to Khashuri, then turn south for Borjomi. From Borjomi the road climbs through forested gorge to Akhaltsikhe, where you turn towards Aspindza and follow the Mtkvari upstream past Khertvisi fortress to Vardzia. The asphalt is good the whole way, but the last 30 km are narrow with blind bends. Fill up in Khashuri or Akhaltsikhe — fuel stations essentially stop after Aspindza. An economy car handles this fine; in winter extra ground clearance is welcome.

### Rabati Castle (Akhaltsikhe)
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/rabati-castle/
Region: Samtskhe-Javakheti | type: fortress | coordinates: 41.6392, 42.9772 | elevation: 1000 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 205 km / 3:20 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~20 ₾ (ზედა ეზო)
Rabati is the historic core of Akhaltsikhe: a walled town on a hill that served for centuries as the seat of the Jaqeli princes and later as the centre of Ottoman administration in the region. The name comes from an Arabic word for a fortified quarter.

The complex was extensively rebuilt in 2011-2012, and that restoration is still argued about. Some of what you walk past is genuinely old, some is modern reconstruction in pale stone with new gardens and terraces. Either way, Rabati remains a rare place in Georgia where the religious layering of Meskheti sits in one enclosure — a mosque with its madrasa, an Orthodox church, a synagogue building and part of the princely palace.

The site splits into two zones:

- the lower free zone — lanes, cafes, souvenir shops, tourist information
- the upper ticketed zone — the citadel, the mosque, the history museum and access to the ramparts

From the upper walls you see the whole town and the ridges of Meskheti. The museum inside covers regional archaeology and the Jaqeli period, and is worth the extra twenty minutes.
Tip: Rabati is the natural break on a Vardzia trip, and it works better on the way back, when you are no longer racing the clock at the cave city. Two hours covers it comfortably. Park at the lot by the lower entrance. In summer the stone courtyards get genuinely hot and shade is scarce; in the evening the lighting makes for good photographs. Cafes, toilets and ATMs are in the lower zone, with shops and fuel in the town itself.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi take the E60 to Khashuri, then head south to Borjomi and continue through the narrow rocky stretch of the Mtkvari valley to Akhaltsikhe — roughly three and a half hours in total. The road is paved and in good condition throughout, though the Borjomi-Akhaltsikhe section is narrow and winding, and ices over in winter. Fuel and ATMs are available in both Borjomi and Akhaltsikhe. An economy car is entirely sufficient; a crossover simply rides the winter road more comfortably.

### Borjomi Central Park and Mineral Springs
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/borjomi-central-park/
Region: Samtskhe-Javakheti | type: spa | coordinates: 41.8378, 43.3856 | elevation: 800 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 160 km / 2:20 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~2 ₾
Borjomi became a Romanov summer residence at the end of the 19th century, and the resort park laid out then is still the heart of the town. Wooden balconies, a bandstand and small bridges line the narrow gorge of the Borjomula river, and the whole place keeps the atmosphere of an imperial-era spa.

Five minutes past the entrance you reach the point of the visit: the original mineral spring, where the water comes out warm and salty. It tastes nothing like the bottled version, and drinking it is free — bring a cup or an empty bottle.

Deeper into the park a path runs along the river and, after two or three kilometres, reaches an open-air pool fed by warm sulphur water, with forest trails starting from the same spot.

What you get:

- the historic alley, pavilions and fountains
- the source spring itself
- a cable car to the plateau above, with a panorama of the gorge
- the thermal pool in the forest, charged separately

Borjomi is also the main gateway to Borjomi-Kharagauli National Park, so many visitors use the town as a base for a night or two.
Tip: The warm, mildly salty taste of the water surprises most first-timers; that is part of the experience. Bring an empty bottle, and swimwear plus a towel if you intend to walk to the thermal pool. The last 300 metres to the gate are on foot — park in the centre near the entrance, as spaces fill quickly in summer. Two or three hours cover the park; add the pool and it becomes half a day. Cafes, toilets and ATMs are all in the town centre.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi take the E60 past Gori to Khashuri, turn south there and cover the last 30 km into Borjomi — about 160 km and two hours twenty in total. The whole route is good asphalt, and the final gorge section is cleared through winter. Fuel is plentiful up to Khashuri and in Borjomi itself. An economy car is fine. If you plan to continue up to Bakuriani the same day, the mountain serpentine is more comfortable in something with clearance, particularly between December and March.

### Borjomi-Kharagauli National Park
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/borjomi-kharagauli-national-park/
Region: Samtskhe-Javakheti | type: nature | coordinates: 41.8283, 43.3339 | elevation: 1100 m | time needed: 6 h | from Tbilisi: 165 km / 2:30 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: may-october | entry: ~15 ₾ (ბილიკები/ღამისთევა ცალკე)
Borjomi-Kharagauli National Park covers roughly one percent of Georgia and is among the largest protected forest areas in Europe. Founded in 1995, it was the first Georgian park set up to international standards: waymarked trails, mountain huts, designated campsites and compulsory registration at a visitor centre.

This is not a drive-up viewpoint. The park is walked, on routes ranging from a couple of hours to eight days.

The usual options:

- short Likani and Atskuri trails — two to four hours from the visitor centre
- day routes — a full day through beech forest into subalpine meadow
- multi-day treks with hut nights, including the Romanov trail, over two or three days

Bears, lynx, red deer and eagles still live in this forest, and higher sections of the trail network cross 2,000 metres, where snow often lingers into June. Even on a short walk the change is obvious: within an hour you go from spa-town parkland into genuinely wild, thickly wooded country with almost no phone signal.

The visitor centre in Borjomi handles registration, maps, trail-condition updates and guide bookings.
Tip: Start at the visitor centre in Borjomi: registration is required, sections close depending on weather, and guides are booked there. Carry water, food, a windproof layer and real hiking boots — conditions change twice a day at this altitude. There is no mobile coverage across much of the trail network. For a day walk, be moving by 09:00. Pack out all rubbish; fires are permitted only at marked sites, and the rule is enforced.
Route from Tbilisi: Take the E60 from Tbilisi to Khashuri, then turn south for Borjomi — 160 km, about two and a half hours. The visitor centre sits in Borjomi on the Likani side of town. Access roads to the individual gates (Likani, Marelisi, Atskuri, Kharagauli) are partly gravel and develop deep ruts after rain, which is why a crossover is the safer choice here. Fill up in Borjomi: there is no fuel and no shop at the trailheads. You need the car only to reach the gate, not beyond it.

### Abastumani Astrophysical Observatory
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/abastumani-observatory/
Region: Samtskhe-Javakheti | type: museum | coordinates: 41.7542, 42.8206 | elevation: 1650 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 235 km / 3:50 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: may-october | entry: ~15 ₾ (ექსკურსია)
Abastumani made its name in the 19th century for dry pine air prescribed against lung disease; Grand Duke George Romanov spent his final years at this resort. The same climate — hundreds of cloudless nights a year — later turned out to be ideal for a very different purpose.

The observatory was founded in 1932 on Mount Kanobili, above the resort at roughly 1,650 metres. It was the first high-altitude astrophysical observatory in the region, and for decades its telescopes were among the principal instruments of Soviet astronomy. Today the site belongs to Ilia State University and still carries out research.

What a visit involves:

- historic telescopes inside their domes, including the large reflector and a meniscus system
- Soviet-era scientific buildings scattered through the forest
- a long view over the Meskheti ridges from the upper terrace

Abastumani itself deserves the stop. Old wooden dachas with carved balconies, sulphur bathhouses and the Otskhe river fill a tight forested valley. The resort is slowly being renovated, but its appeal is precisely that it feels stopped in time, unpolished and quiet in a way few Georgian resorts still manage.

Tours normally run during daylight hours, and in clear weather an evening observing session is sometimes arranged.
Tip: Arrange the visit in advance: this is a working research site and you cannot simply walk in without a guide. Actual observing through a telescope depends entirely on clear skies, so treat an evening session as a bonus rather than a plan. Temperatures drop noticeably above the resort — bring a warm layer even in August. Park on the upper terrace. Cafes and shops exist only down in Abastumani; the nearest ATM is in Akhaltsikhe.
Route from Tbilisi: Follow the E60 from Tbilisi to Khashuri, then head south through Borjomi to Akhaltsikhe. From there turn west and drive about 30 km up a wooded valley to Abastumani — 235 km and close to four hours in total. Asphalt reaches the resort, though it is patchy in places. The final eight kilometres up to the observatory are a steep, narrow serpentine with rough surface, which is why a crossover is the sensible choice. In winter this section can be blocked by snow. Fill up in Akhaltsikhe.

### Khertvisi Fortress
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/khertvisi-fortress/
Region: Samtskhe-Javakheti | type: fortress | coordinates: 41.4769, 43.2864 | elevation: 1100 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 250 km / 4:05 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Khertvisi sits on a narrow rock spur at the confluence of the Mtkvari and the Paravani, exactly where two gorges meet. The name says as much: a place at the junction of rivers. There is no better defensive position in this part of Meskheti, which is why a stronghold has stood here since antiquity.

Folk tradition credits Alexander the Great with destroying the fortress. That is legend rather than history, but it shows how ancient the site was already considered in the Middle Ages. The walls and towers you see today are mostly 14th to 16th century, while the small church on the site is considerably older.

What there is to see:

- high curtain walls and towers that follow the shape of the rock
- the citadel on the upper level
- views over the river confluence and the gorge running on towards Vardzia

The fortress is essentially always open and free to enter. You can climb through it freely, but stairs, ledges and sections of wall are unprotected — there are no railings anywhere, and children need to be held.

Because the Vardzia road passes directly beneath the walls, this stop costs almost nothing in driving time.
Tip: Khertvisi is the natural pause on the drive to Vardzia, and thirty to forty minutes is enough. Leave the car by the bridge at the foot of the rock. The climb goes up a steep stone path that is slippery even in dry weather, so proper shoes matter and sandals are a bad idea. There are no railings, so keep hold of children on the upper walls. No toilets, cafe or ATM here — the nearest are in Aspindza, about fifteen kilometres away.
Route from Tbilisi: The route is the same as for Vardzia: E60 from Tbilisi to Khashuri, south through Borjomi and Akhaltsikhe, then towards Aspindza along the Mtkvari gorge. Khertvisi stands right at the roadside about fifteen kilometres before Vardzia and is visible long before you reach it. Around 250 km and four hours in total. The asphalt is good the whole way, with the last stretch narrow and winding. Fill up in Akhaltsikhe. An economy car is entirely sufficient; nothing here requires clearance.

### Lake Paravani and Lake Tabatskuri
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/paravani-tabatskuri-lakes/
Region: Samtskhe-Javakheti | type: lake | coordinates: 41.45, 43.7833 | elevation: 2073 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 175 km / 3:10 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: june-september | entry: free
The Javakheti plateau is the least touristic landscape in Georgia: a treeless volcanic tableland at around 2,000 metres where nothing interrupts the horizon. Two of the country's most significant high lakes sit on it.

Paravani is the largest lake in Georgia by surface area, roughly 37 square kilometres, yet remarkably shallow — barely three metres at its deepest. It freezes solid in winter. Tabatskuri is the opposite: over forty metres deep, known for its trout, with a wilder and harder-to-reach shoreline.

Both lakes are important stopovers on a migration corridor. In spring and autumn cranes, geese, ducks and even pelicans rest here, and the Javakheti Protected Areas were established largely to safeguard these wetlands.

What to expect:

- vast open views, near-total silence and constant wind
- villages of Armenian and Greek origin along the shores, often built from stone and dung brick
- essentially no infrastructure — no cafe, toilet or shop at the water

This is a destination for travellers who want empty space rather than a checklist of monuments. Photographers come for the light, which on a clear day across an unbroken plateau is unlike anywhere else in the country.
Tip: Paravani sits directly beside the main road and is easy to reach; Tabatskuri involves a gravel track that needs dry weather and decent clearance. Dress warmly even in summer — at 2,000 metres the wind never stops and evening temperatures drop below ten degrees. Carry water and food, since there is no shop at the shore. Fill the tank in Tsalka or Ninotsminda. Almost nobody swims here: the water stays cold through the whole season.
Route from Tbilisi: Head southwest out of Tbilisi on the Tsalka road. It climbs into the hills almost immediately and narrows as it goes. Beyond Tsalka you emerge onto the Javakheti plateau and Paravani appears on the left, right at the roadside. About 175 km and three hours in total. The asphalt is mostly reasonable but broken in places, and the turnoff towards Tabatskuri is gravel. In winter the plateau gets deep snow and severe wind — the route is not recommended between November and April. A crossover is noticeably more comfortable here.

### Sapara Monastery
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/sapara-monastery/
Region: Samtskhe-Javakheti | type: monastery | coordinates: 41.6069, 43.0289 | elevation: 1300 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 215 km / 3:35 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: all | entry: free
Sapara stands southeast of Akhaltsikhe at the end of a tight valley, built onto a terrace in the cliff face. The location was chosen so that the monastery is almost invisible from below — the name itself means hidden. That concealment is largely why it survived while other monasteries of Meskheti were destroyed.

A community existed here by the 9th or 10th century, but Sapara flourished under the Jaqeli princes. At the end of the 13th century Beka Jaqeli built the main church of St Saba, which remains the centre of the complex. Its walls carry painting from the same period, one of the significant surviving examples of medieval Georgian wall art.

Altogether the site holds around a dozen churches and chapels, a bell tower, monastic quarters and partly preserved defensive walls. It is an active monastery with a permanent community of monks.

Worth focusing on:

- the frescoes of St Saba's church and the painted sanctuary
- the view down the valley from the edge of the terrace
- the quiet, which unlike at Vardzia is genuine — coaches rarely make the climb

Sapara is only half an hour from Akhaltsikhe and pairs naturally with a visit to Rabati Castle on the same day.
Tip: This is a working monastery: women need a headscarf and a long skirt, men long trousers, and shorts will not get you in. Photography inside the churches is normally not permitted. Come in the morning or mid-afternoon, and keep quiet during services. Leave the car on the small terrace below the complex and walk the last stretch up. Toilets are basic; there is no cafe and no ATM, with the nearest in Akhaltsikhe about thirty kilometres back.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi take the usual road to Khashuri, then Borjomi and Akhaltsikhe — roughly 215 km and three and a half hours. From Akhaltsikhe turn southeast; the final eight or nine kilometres are a narrow, steep serpentine. Asphalt exists but has collapsed in places, and two cars barely pass each other on the bends, which is why a crossover is the better choice. After rain or in winter this section becomes noticeably harder. Fill up in Akhaltsikhe, because there is nothing at all above the town.

### Uplistsikhe
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/uplistsikhe/
Region: Shida Kartli | type: cave | coordinates: 41.9678, 44.2078 | elevation: 590 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 100 km / 1:25 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~25 ₾
Uplistsikhe was cut out of the rock rather than built on it. East of Gori, on the left bank of the Mtkvari, halls, streets, temples, wine presses and altars were hollowed by hand out of a soft sandstone massif. The town took shape in the first millennium BC and was inhabited from the early Iron Age into the Middle Ages — close to three thousand years of continuous life.

Before Christianity it was a major pagan cult centre. The name means "the lord's fortress", and that double sense, divine and royal, says a good deal about its standing. It sat on a branch of the Silk Road and its wealth came from trade. In the 13th century the Mongols destroyed the town, and it was gradually abandoned.

Around forty of the two hundred-odd caves are open today:

- The Hall of Queen Tamar, the largest space, with a coffered ceiling carved directly into the rock, probably a pagan temple originally
- A secret tunnel down to the river, used to fetch water during sieges
- A three-nave brick basilica from the 9th or 10th century crowning the site
- Wine presses and qvevri pits, some of the oldest winemaking traces in the country

From the top the Mtkvari valley and the Gori plain open out, and at sunset the rock turns orange.
Tip: There is virtually no shade and the rock becomes an oven at midday, so in July and August come before ten in the morning or after five. The surfaces are smooth, polished stone that is dangerously slippery in rain, so wear shoes with grip. The stairs are steep and railings are intermittent, so keep an eye on children. Bring water. The ticket office, toilets and a small café are at the entrance, and hiring a guide on site is genuinely worth it here.
Route from Tbilisi: Leave Tbilisi westwards on the E60 motorway towards Gori — 85 km of fast, good road. Shortly before Gori take the signed Uplistsikhe turning and follow a narrow but asphalted road for a further 14 km over the Kvernaki ridge down to the riverbank. In total about 100 km and an hour and twenty-five minutes. There is a large free car park at the entrance. Fuel and shops are plentiful along the motorway and in Gori. An economy car is entirely sufficient in any season.

### Gori: Fortress and Stalin Museum
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/gori-fortress-stalin-museum/
Region: Shida Kartli | type: town | coordinates: 41.9845, 44.11 | elevation: 570 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 86 km / 1:10 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: მუზეუმი ~20 ₾, ციხე უფასო
Gori tells two very different stories at once. In the middle of town, on an isolated hill rising from a flat plain, stands Gori Fortress. Its walls contain layers going back to the 7th century, though what you see is largely 16th and 17th century. It controlled the confluence of the Mtkvari and the Greater Liakhvi — the main trading knot of Kartli. The 1920 earthquake damaged it badly, but the perimeter walls and the view over the town survive.

Below, on the central avenue, is the Joseph Stalin Museum, opened in 1957. It has three parts: the colonnaded museum building, the small wooden house where Stalin was born, now sheltered under a Greek portico, and his personal armoured railway carriage.

The permanent display has changed little since Soviet times, which is precisely what makes a visit both compelling and uncomfortable. Repression is barely covered; one small room was added in recent years to address it, and the imbalance is impossible to miss.

Beyond these two sights Gori is an ordinary provincial town with a pleasant centre, a market and decent cafés. It also works as the base for Uplistsikhe and the Ateni gorge, both within twenty minutes.
Tip: Hiring a guide in the museum is close to essential: the labelling is thin and much of the display makes little sense without context. English and Russian speaking guides are available on site. The walk up to the fortress takes about ten minutes on a stone path with no handrail, so take care when wet. Allow one to two hours for the museum and an hour for the citadel. Cafés, ATMs and toilets are on Stalin Avenue, and parking in front of the museum is free.
Route from Tbilisi: Gori is 86 km from Tbilisi on the E60 motorway, about an hour and ten minutes on a fast, well-maintained road. The turn-off is clearly signed; once in town follow Stalin Avenue, with the museum and the fortress about ten minutes apart on foot. Leave the car on the large square in front of the museum. Everything is asphalt and any car category will do. Fuel is available on the motorway or at the town entrance, and Uplistsikhe is only 15 km further on.

### Ateni Sioni Church
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/ateni-sioni-church/
Region: Shida Kartli | type: monastery | coordinates: 41.8547, 44.1074 | elevation: 620 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 98 km / 1:30 | road: mostly_paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Ateni Sioni is the younger sibling of Jvari. Built in the 7th century on the same tetraconch plan as the church above Mtskheta, it is generally accepted that its masons were working directly from the Jvari model. It stands south of Gori in the Tana gorge, in a quiet spot enclosed by steep slopes and vineyards.

The real treasure is inside. The surviving 11th-century frescoes are among the finest examples of medieval Georgian painting, particularly the Dormition of the Virgin and the cycle of the life of Christ. The walls also carry very early *asomtavruli* inscriptions, including 8th and 9th century graffiti that historians treat as a source in their own right.

The gorge itself is a reason to come:

- The Ateni vineyards, historic home of *atenuri* wine, with several small cellars working again
- The rock walls of the Tana valley and the river, which keeps the gorge cool in summer
- The ruins of Ateni fortress on a crag a few kilometres beyond the church

Coach tours do not come here. After the crowds at Uplistsikhe, the emptiness of Ateni is a striking and welcome contrast, and the drive up the gorge is pleasant in its own right.
Tip: The church is not always open; the door is often locked with the key kept in a nearby house, and a patient, polite enquiry usually solves it. The frescoes are lit only by daylight, so come in the middle of the day, and flash photography is not allowed. Normal dress rules apply. Facilities in the gorge are minimal, so use cafés and toilets in Gori. Allow an hour for the church and another for a walk along the river.
Route from Tbilisi: Take the E60 from Tbilisi to Gori (86 km, an hour and ten minutes), then turn south out of the town onto the Ateni gorge road and continue about 12 km along the Tana river. The road is mostly asphalt but narrow, with potholed sections and several single-lane bridges — take care after rain. In total roughly 98 km and an hour and a half. An economy car manages it, though a crossover makes the last few kilometres more comfortable. Fill up in Gori, as there is no fuel station in the gorge.

### Kintsvisi Monastery
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/kintsvisi-monastery/
Region: Shida Kartli | type: monastery | coordinates: 41.9864, 43.8264 | elevation: 810 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 125 km / 1:50 | road: mostly_paved | car: suv | season: may-october | entry: free
Kintsvisi holds a place in art history because of one fresco, and that fresco genuinely justifies the detour. On the north wall of St Nicholas church an angel announces the Resurrection to the myrrh-bearing women. The face, the softness of the pigment and the lightness of the gesture depart so far from the period standard that the Angel of Kintsvisi has become the emblem of medieval Georgian painting.

The monastery was built around the turn of the 12th and 13th centuries, in the reign of Queen Tamar, at the peak of the Georgian golden age. Three churches stand in the complex, the main one a brick cross-domed church. Inside there are also portraits of Tamar and her son Giorgi Lasha, which makes the building a historical document as well as an artistic one.

The setting matters too. The monastery sits in dense deciduous forest north of Kareli, above a small valley, and in autumn the colour here is remarkable. It is an active monastery with monks in residence, the silence is close to total, and visitor numbers are low.

Kintsvisi is often skipped simply because it lies fifteen kilometres off the motorway — which is precisely why you tend to have it to yourself.
Tip: The church door is not always open; if you find it locked, ask at the monastic building. The frescoes are lit only by weak natural light, so come on a sunny day around midday, and flash photography is forbidden. The dress code applies and scarves are left by the door. The last kilometres run through forest and turn muddy after rain. There are no facilities at all — buy water, food and fuel in Kareli. Two hours is ample.
Route from Tbilisi: From Tbilisi take the E60 west past Gori to Kareli, about 110 km of fast motorway. Turn north in Kareli and continue 12 to 15 km through villages. Most of that is asphalt, but the final two or three kilometres are narrow, steep and partly gravel through woodland. In total 125 km and roughly an hour and fifty minutes. In dry weather a crossover is comfortable and a sedan is possible with care; after rain you genuinely want ground clearance. Fill up in Gori or Kareli before turning off.

### Samtavisi Cathedral
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/samtavisi-cathedral/
Region: Shida Kartli | type: monastery | coordinates: 41.9086, 44.4328 | elevation: 610 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 62 km / 1:00 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Samtavisi is the building that gave the Georgian church facade its face. It was built in 1030 by Bishop Ilarion Samtavneli, and its eastern front — a large carved cross flanked by rhombuses above a row of decorative arches — became the model that dozens of churches across Kartli and Kakheti reproduced over the next two hundred years.

The decoration is the point here. The composition on that eastern wall is so precisely balanced that art historians treat it as a key monument of medieval Georgian architecture, and it repays standing still for a while. Inside the church is far more restrained, with fresco fragments dating from the 15th to the 17th century.

The complex also includes:

- A curtain wall with towers, partly ruined, on the northern side
- A bell tower and the remains of the bishop's palace
- An old graveyard around the church, with carved stone crosses

The dome was rebuilt after an earthquake in the 15th century and differs slightly in proportion from the original, a detail that is obvious once you look at the church from the side.

Samtavisi lies five kilometres off the main highway and is often empty, yet it is under an hour from Tbilisi — which makes it an ideal first stop on any westward route.
Tip: An hour covers it comfortably. The church is normally open during the day, though a priest is not always present; dress rules apply and scarves are kept by the door. Morning is the best time to photograph the facade, when the sun falls directly on the eastern wall and the carving stands out in relief. Facilities in the village are minimal, so take care of cafés, toilets and fuel in Kaspi or on the motorway.
Route from Tbilisi: Take the E60 motorway west from Tbilisi towards Kaspi, about 55 km. Shortly before Kaspi turn north at the Samtavisi sign and follow an asphalted village road for a further five or six kilometres. In total 62 km and roughly an hour. The cathedral stands in the middle of the village and its walls are visible from a distance; parking at the gate is free. The route is asphalt throughout and an economy car is entirely sufficient. Fuel is available on the motorway or in Kaspi.

### Narikala Fortress
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/narikala-fortress/
Region: Tbilisi | type: fortress | coordinates: 41.6879, 44.8086 | elevation: 430 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 3 km / 0:15 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Narikala is the visual anchor of Tbilisi. Its stone walls run along the Sololaki ridge, visible from almost every corner of the city and floodlit after dark. The first citadel here dates to the 4th century, when a Persian stronghold guarded the crossing of the Mtkvari. Arabs, Seljuks, Mongols and Persians each added a layer; what stands today is largely 16th and 17th century masonry on much older foundations.

In 1827 lightning struck a powder magazine inside the walls and the explosion destroyed a large part of the fortress. That is why Narikala is a half-ruin rather than a restored castle — and that unfinished, weathered quality is exactly what makes it photogenic.

What you actually see up there:

- Two tiers of curtain wall with towers and walkable ledges, opening a full panorama over the city
- St Nicholas Church in the inner courtyard, rebuilt in the 1990s on medieval foundations
- A single sweeping view that takes in Abanotubani, the river bridges, Metekhi and the Sameba cathedral
- The upper gate of the Botanical Garden on the far slope, with a path down to its waterfall
- The aluminium Kartlis Deda (Mother of Georgia) statue, a twenty-minute ridge walk away

There is no ticket office and no closing time. Narikala is an open hillside where sitting on a warm stone and watching the roofs below counts as a full programme.
Tip: Come before 9 in the morning or in the hour before sunset — at midday the stone radiates heat and there is almost no shade. A good pattern is up by cable car from Rike Park and down on foot into Abanotubani, which gives you two completely different perspectives. Wear shoes with grip: the worn steps and wall tops are genuinely slippery when wet. Railings are missing in places, so keep small children close. Toilets and cafés are down in Abanotubani.
Route from Tbilisi: The fortress is ten to fifteen minutes from the city centre by car, but there is effectively no parking at the walls themselves. Two sensible options: leave the car near Gorgasali Square or in the paid lot in Abanotubani and walk up the cobbled lanes, or park at Rike Park and take the cable car across the river. The third approach, the narrow road over the Sololaki ridge above the Botanical Garden, is steep and clogged with tour buses in summer. Any car will do — you are inside the city, so fuel and road surface are non-issues.

### Abanotubani and the Sulphur Baths
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/abanotubani-sulphur-baths/
Region: Tbilisi | type: spa | coordinates: 41.689, 44.8098 | elevation: 400 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 3 km / 0:15 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ნომერი 50–150 ₾ / საათი
Tbilisi is named after this water. *Tbili* means warm, and the springs of Abanotubani still surface at 38–42°C. Legend has it that King Vakhtang Gorgasali found the hot springs while hunting and decided to move his capital here. Historically the quarter was the city's social engine: people bathed, argued business and arranged marriages in the same steamy rooms.

The bathhouses are sunk into the ground, so from street level you only see low brick domes and chimneys — an oddly oriental skyline in the middle of a European-looking city. Each building has its own character:

- Orbeliani (Chreli) Baths, with a blue-tiled Persian facade, the most photographed building in the quarter
- Sulphur and Bochorma baths, plainer, cheaper and full of locals rather than tour groups
- Leghvtakhevi canyon, a narrow gorge with a waterfall five minutes' walk from the domes
- The Juma Mosque and the Armenian cathedral, one block apart — Tbilisi's mixed inheritance in miniature

The procedure is simple: you rent a private room by the hour rather than buying a per-person ticket. Inside there is a hot pool, a wet room and a place to cool down. A *mekise* scrub with a rough mitt costs extra and is worth trying once, if only to understand what locals mean by it.
Tip: Book a room ahead, especially Friday to Sunday evening. Do not go on a completely empty stomach, but do not go straight after a heavy meal either. Towels and slippers are usually rented on site, and swimwear is optional in a private room. Forty to fifty minutes is plenty — longer in sulphur steam affects blood pressure. Plan a slow hour afterwards, because you will not feel like driving immediately. ATMs and cafés are on Gorgasali Square.
Route from Tbilisi: Abanotubani sits in the lower Old Town, just behind Gorgasali Square, signposted from both the Metekhi bridge and the Baratashvili ramp. The lanes are narrow and one-way, so follow the navigation and do not try to drive up to the bathhouse door. The realistic choices are the paid lot on Gorgasali Square or the underground car park at Rike Park, five minutes away across the bridge. Everything is asphalt and any car category works. Finding a space in the evening is harder than getting here in the first place.

### Holy Trinity Cathedral (Sameba)
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/holy-trinity-cathedral-sameba/
Region: Tbilisi | type: monastery | coordinates: 41.6977, 44.818 | elevation: 440 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 5 km / 0:15 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Sameba is modern Tbilisi's boldest architectural statement. Built between 1995 and 2004 as a symbol of post-Soviet religious revival, it rises about a hundred metres from floor to the top of its cross, making it one of the tallest Orthodox churches in the South Caucasus.

The architect, Archil Mindiashvili, took the classic Georgian cross-dome plan and scaled it up enormously. The result divides opinion — critics call it too new, too smooth — but the interior genuinely feels different from an old church. Light drops straight from the dome into an almost empty volume, and the sheer emptiness is the point.

The complex is more than one building:

- The main cathedral with nine chapels, three of them underground
- A free-standing bell tower, the Patriarch's residence, a seminary and a working monastery
- Terraced gardens where the Old Town and the roofs of Avlabari line up in a single frame
- A view that is at its best in the evening, when the cathedral itself is lit

It is worth remembering that Sameba is an active cathedral rather than a monument. You can enter during the liturgy, but wandering with a camera during a service is not welcome, and Sunday mornings are busy with local worshippers rather than visitors.
Tip: The dress code is enforced. Women need a headscarf and a skirt below the knee — wraps are handed out free at the entrance — and men need long trousers; shorts will not get you in. Photography inside is often prohibited, so keep the phone away unless you see others using one. Mornings and evenings are best; the terrace has no shade at midday. An hour is enough for the church and the gardens. Toilets are on site, cafés are near Avlabari metro.
Route from Tbilisi: The cathedral stands in Avlabari on Elia Hill, ten to fifteen minutes from the centre. Follow signs from either the Metekhi or the Baratashvili bridge — the building is visible from almost everywhere, so getting lost is difficult. There is free parking at the lower gate of the compound, though it fills quickly on feast days; the side streets around Avlabari Square are the fallback. The approach is fully paved with a gentle climb, so any car category is fine. The nearest convenient fuel stations are on Ketevan Dedopali Avenue.

### Mtatsminda Park and Funicular
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/mtatsminda-park/
Region: Tbilisi | type: nature | coordinates: 41.6952, 44.7861 | elevation: 730 m | time needed: 3 h | from Tbilisi: 6 km / 0:20 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ფუნიკულიორი ~6 ₾
Mtatsminda is the roof of Tbilisi. From the ridge at 727 metres the whole city unfolds: the line of the Mtkvari, Narikala, the Sameba cathedral and the Trialeti mountains on the far horizon. It is the one place where the actual scale of Tbilisi becomes obvious.

The funicular opened in 1905 to a Belgian design and still runs on its original alignment. There are three stations: the lower one on Chonkadze Street, an intermediate stop at the Mtatsminda Pantheon, where Ilia Chavchavadze, Akaki Tsereteli, Niko Pirosmani and the Russian writer Griboyedov are buried, and the upper station inside the park.

The park itself is several things at once:

- A Ferris wheel built right on the edge of the ridge, which puts the view underneath you
- Rides and carousels for children, plus small themed zones
- Restaurant terraces that are the best sunset seats in the city
- Woodland paths for anyone who wants to escape the noise of the fairground
- The television tower, floodlit at night and used by locals as a navigation point

In winter part of the park keeps working, though some rides close. The view, on the other hand, is far sharper in cold air than in the summer haze.
Tip: Arrive about two hours before sunset and you get the daytime city, the golden hour and the night city in a single visit. Rides are paid with a rechargeable card bought at the entrance, so load enough if you are with children. The ridge is windy and four to six degrees cooler than the centre — bring a jacket even in summer. Queues for the funicular are long on weekend evenings, so driving up can actually be faster. Toilets and cafés are inside the park.
Route from Tbilisi: There are two ways up. The first is the funicular from Chonkadze Street, leaving your car in the surrounding streets. The second is to drive the Mtatsminda switchbacks from the Vake or Turtle Lake side: narrow but fully asphalted, about twenty minutes from the centre, with a large free car park at the top. In winter the climb can be awkward when the surface ices over, so after snowfall the funicular is the reliable option. In normal conditions an economy car handles the road without any trouble.

### Georgian National Museum
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/georgian-national-museum/
Region: Tbilisi | type: museum | coordinates: 41.695, 44.8 | elevation: 410 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 2 km / 0:10 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~15 ₾
One building that holds the whole of Georgian history. The Simon Janashia Museum on Rustaveli Avenue is the main branch of the National Museum network, and if you only have time for one museum in the country, this is the one to choose.

Two collections here are genuinely world class. The first is the Treasury in the basement: gold jewellery from the third millennium BC onwards, Colchian and Iberian work in sheet gold and granulation so fine that modern goldsmiths struggle to reproduce it. These are the objects that sit behind the myth of the Argonauts and the Golden Fleece, and seeing them makes the legend feel a good deal less like fiction.

The second is the Dmanisi collection: hominid skulls roughly 1.8 million years old, the earliest human remains found outside Africa. This is a discovery of global significance, and the museum presents it properly rather than as a footnote.

The rest of the permanent display covers:

- The Museum of Soviet Occupation, documenting repression between 1921 and 1991
- An archaeology floor running from the Bronze Age to the Middle Ages
- Ethnographic and numismatic collections
- Temporary exhibitions, often contemporary art

Labels are in Georgian and English. Russian captions are patchy, so an audio guide or a live guide is worth the extra cost if you want more than the objects themselves.
Tip: The Treasury often needs a separate ticket or a timed slot — ask at the desk on arrival and go down there first, before the tour groups. Two hours is a realistic minimum and three is comfortable. Large bags must be left in the cloakroom. Since the museum is right in the centre, pair it with a walk along Rustaveli. There is a café and toilets inside the building and plenty of ATMs on the avenue.
Route from Tbilisi: The museum stands on Rustaveli Avenue opposite parliament, five minutes' walk from Freedom Square. Driving here is easy; parking is not. Stopping on the avenue itself is usually prohibited and tow trucks are active. The sensible answer is one of the paid underground or courtyard car parks on Chitadze, Lermontov or Ingorokva street. The alternative is to leave the car at your hotel and take the metro to Rustaveli station, which during rush hour is genuinely faster. Everything is asphalt, so any car category is fine.

### Open Air Museum of Ethnography
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/open-air-museum-of-ethnography/
Region: Tbilisi | type: museum | coordinates: 41.7106, 44.7565 | elevation: 620 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 8 km / 0:20 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: ~10 ₾
This is Georgia compressed into an hour's walk. On a wooded hillside above Vake, on the way up to Turtle Lake, 52 hectares hold real houses that were dismantled in their home villages and reassembled here. The museum was founded in 1966 on the initiative of the ethnographer Giorgi Chitaia.

The path is organised into zones, each representing a historical province:

- Kartli and Kakheti — *darbazi* houses with a central hearth and a stepped smoke hole, plus wine cellars with buried qvevri
- Svaneti — a defensive stone tower and a *machubi*, the single room where family and cattle wintered together
- Samegrelo and Guria — timber houses raised off the ground against damp
- Adjara and Imereti — wooden buildings with wide balconies and ingenious internal water systems
- Khevsureti and Tusheti — dry stone mountain structures built without mortar

Most interiors are fully furnished with pots, rugs, beds and tools, and in several houses an attendant will explain how the space was actually used through the year.

The museum doubles as a park: shade, old trees, quiet paths. In summer it is several degrees cooler than the city, which is a reason to come in itself, and in late October the whole slope turns yellow.
Tip: The site is large and the paths run up and down the slope, so wear comfortable shoes — heels are hopeless here. After rain the ground turns muddy and some sections puddle badly. Two hours covers the main zones, three covers everything. Bring water: the on-site café is small and not always open. Children enjoy the houses, but a pushchair is hard work on these paths. Early morning or an autumn afternoon are the best times.
Route from Tbilisi: From the centre take Chavchavadze Avenue through Vake, then the road climbing towards Turtle Lake — about twenty minutes in normal traffic. The museum entrance is on the right, roughly a kilometre before the lake, and clearly signposted. There is free parking at the gate, which can fill at weekends. The climb is asphalt and open all year; it demands some care when it ices over in winter, but an economy car is entirely adequate. Fill up on Chavchavadze Avenue or at the top end of Vake.

### Turtle Lake and Vake Park
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/turtle-lake-vake-park/
Region: Tbilisi | type: lake | coordinates: 41.7089, 44.7503 | elevation: 686 m | time needed: 2 h | from Tbilisi: 9 km / 0:20 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Turtle Lake belongs to the locals. It rarely tops a visitor's list, and that is precisely why it delivers something the Old Town cannot: ordinary, unperformed Tbilisi. The small lake sits at 686 metres on a pine-covered ridge above Vake.

Vake Park below was laid out in 1946 and is a textbook Soviet park — broad alleys, a fountain, a cascade of steps. From its upper end a cable car climbs to the lake in about five minutes, with the whole district dropping away beneath you.

What people do at Turtle Lake:

- Walk the flat lakeside loop, roughly a kilometre around
- Rent a pedalo or rowing boat in the warm months
- Sit in the terraced cafés looking out over the water towards the ridge
- Walk down to the Open Air Museum of Ethnography, about twenty minutes on a woodland path
- In winter, simply walk: the lake often freezes at the edges and the pine forest goes quiet

Because the ridge is one of the coolest spots in Tbilisi, half the city comes up here during the July and August heat. Mid-week is when you get the place closer to how it feels the rest of the year, and the light on the water in late afternoon is worth the trip on its own.
Tip: In summer the lakeside cafés fill after five in the afternoon and parking becomes the main problem — either come early or take the cable car up from Vake Park instead. The lake is not an official swimming spot even though people do swim; there is no supervised beach. Dress for the evening drop in temperature up here. ATMs are down on Chavchavadze, and not every kiosk by the lake takes cards. With children this is one of the easiest days out in the city.
Route from Tbilisi: Follow Chavchavadze Avenue to Vake Park, then either leave the car at the park and ride the cable car, or keep driving the switchbacks straight to the lake — both take up to twenty minutes from the centre. There is free parking around the lake, though on summer evenings it is full and the narrow road makes passing awkward. The surface is asphalt the whole way. In winter the climb needs careful driving when it ices over, but no four-wheel drive is required; an economy car is enough.

### The Chronicle of Georgia
URL: https://www.example.ge/en/attractions/chronicle-of-georgia/
Region: Tbilisi | type: museum | coordinates: 41.7666, 44.808 | elevation: 570 m | time needed: 1 h | from Tbilisi: 14 km / 0:30 | road: paved | car: economy | season: all | entry: free
Sixteen pillars, each about sixteen metres tall, standing on an empty hill. Zurab Tsereteli began this monument in 1985 and it has never been finished, which is part of why the site feels so strange and so cinematic. It rarely appears in printed guidebooks and constantly appears on Instagram.

The lower half of each column carries relief figures of Georgian kings, queens, heroes and poets, from Vakhtang Gorgasali to Shota Rustaveli. The upper half is given to biblical scenes: the Nativity, the Crucifixion, the Resurrection. National history and sacred history meet at the two ends of the same vertical, an idea Tsereteli returned to throughout his career.

From the edge of the hill the view opens over the Tbilisi Sea, the large reservoir that supplies the city, with wind turbines on the ridges and dry steppe hills beyond. The landscape looks nothing like the rest of Tbilisi and rather more like Central Asia.

One practical truth: the place is essentially unmanaged. There is no ticket, no real infrastructure, no lighting after dark, and the concrete platform is cracked in places. That is neither a flaw nor a virtue, simply what it is — and the reason it is often almost empty when you arrive.
Tip: Come in the hour before sunset: the columns face west and the bronze catches fire in that light. Do not linger after dark, since there is no lighting and the surfaces are uneven. There is no shade at all in summer and the wind is constant, so bring a hat and water. No toilets, café or ATM on site — the nearest facilities are along the Tbilisi Sea road. An hour is more than enough time here, unless you are photographing.
Route from Tbilisi: The monument stands on the northern edge of the city near the western shore of the Tbilisi Sea. From the centre take George Bush Street or the Tbilisi Sea road, roughly 25 to 30 minutes. The last two kilometres are narrow, patched asphalt with potholes, but perfectly passable. Navigation apps sometimes suggest a poor turning, so use the Tbilisi Sea shore road and its upper branch as your reference. Parking is free right at the columns. An economy car copes, though a crossover makes the last stretch more comfortable.
